subject: Pathology I
question: Explain cell injury. Compare reversible and irreversible cell injury.

diagram.caption: Changes in reversible and irreversible cell injury

answer_html:
Definition Cell injury is the sequence of changes that occur when a cell is exposed to a stress or harmful agent beyond its capacity to adapt. If the stimulus is mild or brief, the injury is reversible; if it is severe or persistent, the cell passes a "point of no return" and dies (irreversible injury → necrosis or apoptosis).

1. Causes of cell injury

  1. Hypoxia and ischaemia – the commonest cause (atherosclerosis, thrombosis, anaemia, shock, respiratory failure, CO poisoning).
  2. Physical agents – trauma, burns, frostbite, radiation, electric shock, sudden pressure changes.
  3. Chemicals and drugs – poisons (cyanide, organophosphates), alcohol, paracetamol overdose, carbon tetrachloride, even excess oxygen or glucose.
  4. Infectious agents – bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites and their toxins.
  5. Immunological reactions – autoimmune diseases, hypersensitivity (anaphylaxis).
  6. Genetic defects – sickle cell anaemia, enzyme deficiencies.
  7. Nutritional imbalances – protein-energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiencies; obesity and excess fat.
  8. Ageing.

2. Mechanisms (in brief)

  • Depletion of ATP (failure of the Na⁺/K⁺ pump, anaerobic glycolysis, lactic acid).
  • Mitochondrial damage.
  • Influx of calcium activating destructive enzymes.
  • Free radicals (reactive oxygen species) damaging membranes, proteins and DNA.
  • Membrane damage and DNA/protein damage.

3. Reversible cell injury

  • Cellular (hydropic) swelling – first change; failure of the sodium pump lets water enter the cell.
  • Fatty change (steatosis) – accumulation of lipid droplets, e.g., liver in alcoholism, heart in hypoxia.
  • Swollen mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum, detachment of ribosomes, loss of microvilli, membrane blebs, clumping of nuclear chromatin.
  • Function is reduced, but the cell recovers if the cause is removed.

4. Irreversible cell injury

  • Severe mitochondrial damage (amorphous densities) – no ATP production.
  • Extensive damage to plasma membrane – leakage of cell enzymes into blood.
  • Rupture of lysosomes – enzymes digest the cell.
  • Nuclear changes: pyknosis (shrinkage and darkening), karyorrhexis (fragmentation), karyolysis (fading/dissolution).
  • Ends in cell death (necrosis).

5. Comparison | Feature | Reversible injury | Irreversible injury | |---|---|---| | Severity/duration of stimulus | Mild, short | Severe, prolonged | | Cell size | Swollen | Swollen, then ruptures | | Mitochondria | Swollen | Severe damage, densities | | Plasma membrane | Blebs, intact | Ruptured | | Lysosomes | Intact | Ruptured, enzymes released | | Nucleus | Chromatin clumping | Pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis | | ATP | Reduced | Severely depleted | | Enzyme leakage into blood | Absent/minimal | Present (troponin, CK-MB, ALT) | | Outcome | Recovery | Cell death (necrosis) |

6. Clinical significance

  • Enzymes leaking from irreversibly injured cells are used as diagnostic markers – troponin in myocardial infarction, ALT/AST in hepatitis, CK in muscle injury.
  • Early restoration of blood flow (thrombolysis in MI, early stroke treatment) can save cells while injury is still reversible – "time is muscle/brain".

Conclusion Cell injury progresses from reversible swelling and fatty change to irreversible membrane and nuclear damage; recognising and correcting the cause early can prevent cell death.

subject: Pathology I
question: Define necrosis. Describe the types of necrosis with examples.
answer_html:
Definition Necrosis is the death of a group of cells or tissue in a living body, resulting from irreversible injury, accompanied by enzymatic digestion of the dead cells and an inflammatory reaction in the surrounding tissue.

Morphological features

  • Cytoplasm – increased eosinophilia (pink), loss of glycogen, vacuolation.
  • Nucleus – pyknosis, karyorrhexis and karyolysis.
  • Loss of cell outline; inflammatory cells around the dead area.

Types of necrosis 1. Coagulative necrosis

  • Commonest type; the basic outline of dead cells and tissue architecture is preserved for some days ("ghost cells") because proteins and enzymes are denatured.
  • Cause: ischaemia (sudden loss of blood supply).
  • Examples: infarcts of heart (myocardial infarction), kidney, spleen – all solid organs except the brain.

2. Liquefactive (colliquative) necrosis

  • Dead tissue is digested by enzymes into a liquid, viscous mass.
  • Causes: bacterial and fungal infections (enzymes of neutrophils), ischaemia in the brain.
  • Examples: abscesses (pus), brain infarcts (cystic cavity after stroke).

3. Caseous necrosis

  • A combination of coagulative and liquefactive necrosis; gross appearance is soft, friable, cheese-like (caseous), white-yellow.
  • Microscopy – amorphous pink granular debris surrounded by a granuloma (epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes).
  • Example: tuberculosis (also some fungal infections).

4. Fat necrosis

  • (a) Enzymatic fat necrosis – in acute pancreatitis, released lipases digest fat; fatty acids combine with calcium to form chalky white areas (fat saponification); may cause hypocalcaemia.
  • (b) Traumatic fat necrosis – breast after injury (can mimic a lump/cancer).

5. Fibrinoid necrosis

  • Deposition of immune complexes and fibrin in walls of blood vessels – bright pink, smudgy appearance.
  • Examples: vasculitis (polyarteritis nodosa, SLE), malignant hypertension, Aschoff bodies in rheumatic fever.

6. Gangrenous necrosis (clinical term)

  • Necrosis (usually coagulative) of a limb or bowel with superadded putrefaction – dry, wet and gas gangrene (e.g., diabetic foot, strangulated hernia, Clostridium perfringens infection).

Fate of necrotic tissue Removal by phagocytes and enzymes → healing by fibrosis (scar); dystrophic calcification (e.g., in old TB lesions); cavity or cyst formation (brain); infection.

Nursing relevance Early reperfusion (MI, limb ischaemia), proper wound debridement, drainage of abscesses, and prevention of pressure necrosis (pressure ulcers) by regular turning.

Conclusion Necrosis takes different forms depending on the cause and tissue – coagulative in infarcts, liquefactive in abscesses and brain, caseous in TB and fat necrosis in pancreatitis.

subject: Pathology I
question: Differentiate between apoptosis and necrosis.
answer_html:
Introduction Cells die in two main ways. Necrosis is accidental, uncontrolled death caused by severe injury, always pathological. Apoptosis is programmed cell death – an orderly "cell suicide" that removes unwanted, damaged or aged cells without inflammation. Apoptosis is essential for normal development and for protection against cancer.

Apoptosis – definition and mechanism

  • Apoptosis (Greek: "falling off", like leaves) is a regulated, energy-dependent process in which the cell activates enzymes (caspases) that degrade its own DNA and proteins.
  • Triggered by intrinsic (mitochondrial) pathway – DNA damage, lack of growth factors (regulated by BCL-2 family) – or extrinsic (death-receptor) pathway – Fas ligand, TNF.
  • The cell shrinks, chromatin condenses and fragments, and the cell breaks into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies, which are quickly eaten by macrophages.

Differences | Feature | Apoptosis | Necrosis | |---|---|---| | Nature | Programmed, regulated "cell suicide" | Accidental, uncontrolled "cell murder" | | Occurrence | Physiological and pathological | Always pathological | | Stimulus | Mild injury, hormones, DNA damage, immune killing | Severe injury – ischaemia, toxins, infection, burns | | Extent | Single cells or small clusters | Groups of cells, large areas | | Energy (ATP) | Required (active process) | Not required (ATP depletion) | | Cell size | Shrinks | Swells | | Nucleus | Chromatin condensation, fragmentation (orderly) | Pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis (random) | | Plasma membrane | Intact (blebbing) | Ruptured | | Cell contents | Packed in apoptotic bodies | Leak out | | Inflammation | Absent | Present | | DNA on electrophoresis | "Ladder" pattern | Diffuse smear | | Examples | Embryonic development (loss of web between fingers), shedding of endometrium, thymus involution, killing of virus-infected cells by T cells, Councilman bodies in viral hepatitis, tumour cells after radiotherapy/chemotherapy | Myocardial infarction, tuberculosis, abscess, acute pancreatitis, gangrene |

Clinical significance

  • Too little apoptosis – cancer (cells with damaged DNA survive; e.g., overexpression of BCL-2, mutation of p53), autoimmune diseases.
  • Too much apoptosis – neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), ischaemic injury, loss of CD4 cells in HIV.
  • Many anticancer drugs and radiotherapy act by inducing apoptosis.

Nursing relevance Raised cardiac enzymes after MI reflect necrosis; tumour shrinkage after chemotherapy or radiotherapy reflects apoptosis of cancer cells – nurses should watch for tumour lysis effects (high uric acid and potassium) when large tumours break down rapidly.

Conclusion Apoptosis is neat, silent, programmed death of single cells, while necrosis is messy, inflammatory death of tissue due to severe injury.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the cellular adaptations with examples.
answer_html:
Introduction When cells face stress (increased workload, hormonal stimulation, reduced nutrition, chronic irritation), they may adapt by changing their size, number or type. These adaptations allow survival; if the stress exceeds the adaptive capacity, cell injury follows. Adaptations are usually reversible when the stimulus is removed.

1. Hypertrophy – increase in the size of cells

  • Leads to increase in organ size, without new cells; occurs in cells that cannot divide (heart, skeletal muscle).
  • Physiological: skeletal muscle in athletes and labourers; uterus in pregnancy (with hyperplasia).
  • Pathological: left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertension and aortic stenosis; hypertrophy of the bladder wall in prostatic obstruction.

2. Hyperplasia – increase in the number of cells

  • Occurs in cells capable of division.
  • Physiological: hormonal – breast enlargement at puberty and lactation, endometrium in the menstrual cycle; compensatory – regeneration of liver after partial removal.
  • Pathological: endometrial hyperplasia (excess oestrogen – may progress to cancer), benign prostatic hyperplasia, thyroid hyperplasia in Graves' disease, skin warts (virus).

3. Atrophy – decrease in the size of cells and organ

  • Causes: disuse (limb in plaster, bed rest), denervation (polio, nerve injury), reduced blood supply (brain in atherosclerosis), malnutrition (marasmus, cancer cachexia), loss of hormonal stimulation (endometrium, breast after menopause), pressure (tumour pressing tissue), ageing (senile atrophy of brain).

4. Metaplasia – change of one adult cell type to another

  • A reversible change in which one differentiated cell type is replaced by another type better able to withstand stress.
  • Squamous metaplasia – ciliated columnar epithelium of bronchi changes to squamous epithelium in smokers and vitamin A deficiency; cervix (transformation zone).
  • Columnar (glandular) metaplasia – Barrett's oesophagus in chronic acid reflux.
  • Osseous metaplasia (bone formation in soft tissue).
  • Significance: loss of protective function (mucus, cilia) and risk of progression to dysplasia and cancer (lung, oesophagus).

5. Dysplasia – disordered growth (not a true adaptation)

  • Loss of uniformity and orientation of cells, variation in size and shape (pleomorphism), large dark nuclei, increased mitoses.
  • Usually in epithelium after chronic irritation or infection (e.g., HPV in cervix – cervical intraepithelial neoplasia).
  • Mild dysplasia may regress; severe dysplasia (carcinoma in situ) is precancerous.

Summary table | Adaptation | Change | Example | |---|---|---| | Hypertrophy | ↑ cell size | Heart in hypertension | | Hyperplasia | ↑ cell number | Endometrial hyperplasia, BPH | | Atrophy | ↓ cell size | Muscle after immobilisation | | Metaplasia | Change of cell type | Bronchial squamous metaplasia in smokers | | Dysplasia | Disordered growth | CIN in cervix |

Nursing relevance Early mobilisation and exercises prevent disuse atrophy; smoking cessation reverses metaplasia; Pap/VIA screening detects dysplasia early.

Conclusion Hypertrophy, hyperplasia, atrophy and metaplasia are adaptive responses; dysplasia is a warning sign of possible malignancy.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the vascular and cellular events in acute inflammation, with its chemical mediators.

diagram.caption: Sequence of leukocyte events in acute inflammation

answer_html:
Definition Inflammation is the protective response of vascularised living tissue to injury, aimed at destroying or walling off the injurious agent and preparing for repair. Acute inflammation is of short duration (minutes to a few days) and is characterised by exudation of fluid and plasma proteins (oedema) and emigration of neutrophils.

Cardinal signs Rubor (redness), calor (heat), tumor (swelling), dolor (pain) – described by Celsus – and functio laesa (loss of function) added by Virchow.

Causes Infections, trauma, burns, chemicals, necrosis, foreign bodies, immune reactions.

A. Vascular events

  1. Transient vasoconstriction of arterioles (seconds).
  2. Vasodilation – increased blood flow → redness and heat (hyperaemia).
  3. Increased vascular permeability – endothelial cells contract and gaps appear; protein-rich fluid (exudate) escapes into tissues → swelling (oedema).
  4. Slowing of circulation (stasis) – blood becomes concentrated; leukocytes move to the periphery of the vessel.

B. Cellular events (leukocyte events)

  1. Margination – white cells move to the vessel wall.
  2. Rolling – loose binding to endothelium through selectins.
  3. Adhesion – firm attachment via integrins.
  4. Transmigration (diapedesis) – neutrophils squeeze between endothelial cells into tissues (neutrophils in the first 6–24 hours, monocytes/macrophages in 24–48 hours).
  5. Chemotaxis – directed movement towards the site of injury, attracted by bacterial products, C5a, leukotriene B4, IL-8.
  6. Phagocytosis – recognition and attachment (helped by opsonins – IgG and C3b), engulfment into phagosome, killing by reactive oxygen species (respiratory burst, myeloperoxidase) and lysosomal enzymes, and degradation.
  7. Release of enzymes and mediators – may also damage tissue.

C. Chemical mediators | Mediator | Source | Main actions | |---|---|---| | Histamine, serotonin | Mast cells, platelets | Vasodilation, ↑ permeability (immediate) | | Prostaglandins | Arachidonic acid (COX pathway) | Vasodilation, pain, fever (blocked by NSAIDs) | | Leukotrienes | Arachidonic acid (LOX pathway) | Chemotaxis (LTB4), ↑ permeability, bronchospasm | | Cytokines – IL-1, TNF, IL-6 | Macrophages | Fever, acute-phase proteins, leukocytosis, endothelial activation | | Chemokines (IL-8) | Many cells | Chemotaxis | | Complement – C3a, C5a, C3b, MAC | Plasma | Anaphylatoxins (↑ permeability), chemotaxis, opsonisation, cell lysis | | Bradykinin | Plasma kinin system | ↑ permeability, pain | | Platelet-activating factor, nitric oxide | Leukocytes, endothelium | Permeability, vasodilation |

D. Systemic effects Fever, leukocytosis (neutrophilia), raised C-reactive protein and ESR, malaise, anorexia.

E. Outcomes Complete resolution, abscess formation, healing by fibrosis (scar), or progression to chronic inflammation.

Nursing relevance Cold applications and elevation in early injury, warm compresses later, rest of the part, NSAIDs for pain and fever as ordered, and monitoring of temperature and WBC count.

Conclusion Acute inflammation is a rapid vascular and cellular response, orchestrated by chemical mediators, that destroys the injurious agent and paves the way for healing.

subject: Pathology I
question: Write a note on granulomatous inflammation.

diagram.caption: Structure of a tuberculous granuloma
labels: Langhans giant cells with horseshoe nuclei

answer_html:
Introduction Chronic inflammation is inflammation of prolonged duration (weeks to years) in which active inflammation, tissue destruction and attempts at repair go on together; it is marked by mononuclear cells (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells), angiogenesis and fibrosis. Granulomatous inflammation is a distinctive pattern of chronic inflammation.

1. Definition Granulomatous inflammation is a type of chronic inflammation characterised by the formation of granulomas – focal, compact collections of activated macrophages transformed into epithelioid cells, often with multinucleated giant cells, surrounded by a collar of lymphocytes (and plasma cells, fibroblasts).

2. Formation (pathogenesis)

  1. A persistent, poorly degradable agent (e.g., M. tuberculosis, foreign material) is engulfed by macrophages but not destroyed.
  2. Antigen is presented to CD4 T-helper (Th1) cells, which release interferon-gamma.
  3. Interferon-gamma activates macrophages, which enlarge and become epithelioid cells (pale, elongated, slipper-shaped nuclei).
  4. Some epithelioid cells fuse to form giant cells:
    • Langhans giant cells – nuclei arranged in a horseshoe at the periphery (typical of TB).
    • Foreign-body giant cells – nuclei scattered.
  5. Lymphocytes surround the collection; fibroblasts lay down collagen at the periphery; in TB the centre undergoes caseous necrosis.

3. Types and causes (a) Immune granulomas (cell-mediated immunity against persistent antigens)

  • Tuberculosis – caseating granulomas (prototype).
  • Leprosy (tuberculoid type).
  • Syphilis – gumma.
  • Fungal infections – histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis.
  • Sarcoidosis – non-caseating granulomas.

  • Crohn's disease, cat-scratch disease, schistosomiasis. (b) Foreign-body granulomas

  • Around sutures, talc, silica, splinters, surgical gauze, injected drugs – non-immune, foreign-body giant cells.

4. Significance

  • Granulomas wall off organisms the body cannot destroy, limiting spread.
  • But they cause tissue damage, fibrosis, calcification and loss of function (e.g., lung fibrosis, cavities in TB).
  • Diagnosis: biopsy shows granulomas – special stains (Ziehl–Neelsen for AFB, fungal stains), culture, PCR; caseation suggests TB in India.

5. Nursing relevance Assisting in biopsy/FNAC, sending tissue in correct fixative (10% formalin) and a separate fresh sample for culture, and ensuring completion of anti-TB treatment.

6. Caseating versus non-caseating granulomas | Caseating | Non-caseating | |---|---| | Central cheesy necrosis | No necrosis | | Tuberculosis, some fungal infections | Sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease, foreign bodies, leprosy (tuberculoid) |

Conclusion Granulomatous inflammation is the body's way of containing persistent agents like the tubercle bacillus through organised collections of activated macrophages and lymphocytes.

subject: Pathology I
question: Differentiate between healing by first intention and healing by second intention. Mention the factors affecting wound healing.

diagram.caption: Healing by first and second intention
labels: clean incised wound with apposed edges – thin scar; open wound with tissue loss – large granulation tissue

answer_html:
Introduction Wound healing is the process by which injured tissue is repaired by regeneration (replacement by similar cells) and repair by connective tissue (scar formation). The stages of tissue repair (haemostasis, inflammation, proliferation and remodelling) were studied in physiology; pathology describes two patterns of healing that depend on the nature of the wound.

A. Healing by first intention (primary union)

  • Occurs in clean, uninfected, surgical incisions where the edges are approximated by sutures, with minimal tissue loss.
  • Sequence:
    • Day 0–1: blood clot fills the narrow gap; neutrophils appear; epidermal cells start migrating.
    • Day 3: macrophages replace neutrophils; granulation tissue begins.
    • Day 5: maximum new blood vessels; collagen bridges the incision; epidermis restored.
    • Week 2: collagen accumulates; inflammation subsides.
    • End of first month: a thin linear scar; tensile strength increases slowly (about 70–80% of normal by 3 months).

B. Healing by second intention (secondary union)

  • Occurs in wounds with large tissue loss, gaping edges, infection, abscesses, burns, ulcers and pressure sores.
  • More inflammation, abundant granulation tissue fills the defect from the base upwards.
  • Wound contraction by myofibroblasts reduces the size of the wound.
  • Ends in a large, irregular scar; takes longer.

C. Differences | Feature | First intention | Second intention | |---|---|---| | Type of wound | Clean, incised, sutured | Open, infected, with tissue loss | | Wound edges | Approximated | Separated (gaping) | | Tissue loss | Minimal | Extensive | | Inflammation | Mild | Intense | | Granulation tissue | Scanty | Abundant | | Wound contraction | Absent/minimal | Prominent | | Infection | Absent | Often present | | Time to heal | Short | Long | | Scar | Thin, linear | Broad, irregular, may contract | | Example | Surgical incision | Abscess, burns, pressure ulcer, diabetic ulcer | (Delayed primary closure – a contaminated wound is left open for a few days and then sutured – is sometimes called third intention.)

D. Factors affecting wound healing Local factors

  • Infection – the most important cause of delayed healing.
  • Poor blood supply (atherosclerosis, varicose veins), foreign bodies (dirt, sutures), necrotic tissue.

  • Movement and mechanical stress, size and location of wound, haematoma, radiation exposure. Systemic factors

  • Age (slower in elderly), nutrition – protein, vitamin C (collagen synthesis), zinc.

  • Diabetes mellitus, corticosteroids, anaemia, hypoxia, obesity, smoking.
  • Immunosuppression, chemotherapy, jaundice, uraemia.

E. Complications of wound healing Wound infection, wound dehiscence (bursting open) and incisional hernia, hypertrophic scar and keloid, contracture, chronic ulcer, sinus/fistula, rarely squamous cell carcinoma in a chronic scar (Marjolin's ulcer).

Nursing relevance Aseptic dressing, adequate nutrition and glycaemic control, offloading pressure, early detection of infection and patient education promote healing.

Conclusion Clean sutured wounds heal quickly by first intention, while open or infected wounds heal slowly by second intention; controlling local and systemic factors ensures good healing.

subject: Pathology I
question: Define neoplasia. Explain the nomenclature of tumours and the differences between benign and malignant tumours.
answer_html:
Definition Neoplasia means "new growth". A neoplasm (tumour) is "an abnormal mass of tissue, the growth of which exceeds and is uncoordinated with that of the normal tissues, and persists in the same excessive manner after cessation of the stimuli which evoked the change" (Willis). Oncology is the study of tumours; cancer refers to malignant tumours.

A. Nomenclature (naming) of tumours 1. Benign tumours – suffix "-oma" added to the cell of origin:

  • Lipoma (fat), fibroma (fibrous tissue), leiomyoma (smooth muscle – "fibroid" of uterus), adenoma (gland), papilloma (finger-like projections of epithelium), osteoma, chondroma, haemangioma.

2. Malignant tumours

  • Carcinoma – malignant tumour of epithelial origin: squamous cell carcinoma (skin, oral cavity, cervix), adenocarcinoma (glandular – stomach, colon, breast, lung), transitional cell carcinoma (bladder).
  • Sarcoma – malignant tumour of mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin: osteosarcoma, liposarcoma, fibrosarcoma, leiomyosarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma.
  • Tumours of blood cells – leukaemias, lymphomas.

3. Exceptions and special terms

  • Malignant tumours ending in "-oma": lymphoma, melanoma, seminoma, mesothelioma, hepatoma.
  • Teratoma – tumour from germ cells containing tissues of more than one germ layer (hair, teeth).
  • Tumour-like non-neoplastic masses: hamartoma (disorganised normal tissue of that site), choristoma (normal tissue at an abnormal site).
  • Carcinoma in situ – malignant cells confined to the epithelium, not invading the basement membrane.

B. Differences between benign and malignant tumours | Feature | Benign tumour | Malignant tumour | |---|---|---| | Differentiation | Well differentiated – resembles tissue of origin | Varies – well to poorly differentiated; anaplasia (lack of differentiation) | | Rate of growth | Slow | Rapid, erratic | | Mode of growth | Expansile, pushes surrounding tissue | Infiltrative, invasive | | Capsule | Usually encapsulated | Not encapsulated | | Metastasis | Absent | Present – hallmark of malignancy | | Recurrence after removal | Rare | Common | | Nuclei | Normal, uniform | Pleomorphic, hyperchromatic, high nuclear–cytoplasmic ratio, prominent nucleoli | | Mitoses | Few, normal | Many, abnormal (atypical) | | Necrosis, haemorrhage | Rare | Common | | Effect on host | Usually local pressure effects; rarely fatal (except brain) | Cachexia, anaemia, organ failure, death if untreated | | Examples | Lipoma, fibroadenoma, leiomyoma | Carcinoma breast, osteosarcoma, leukaemia |

C. Clinical features of malignancy (warning signs – "CAUTION") Change in bowel/bladder habits, A sore that does not heal, Unusual bleeding or discharge, Thickening or lump, Indigestion or difficulty swallowing, Obvious change in a wart or mole, Nagging cough or hoarseness.

Nursing relevance Health education on early warning signs, screening (oral visual examination, VIA for cervix, clinical breast examination under the NP-NCD programme), and psychological support.

Conclusion Tumours are named by tissue of origin and behaviour; invasion and metastasis distinguish malignant from benign tumours.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the routes of spread (metastasis) of malignant tumours. Add a note on grading and staging of cancer.

diagram.caption: Routes of spread of malignant tumours
labels: local invasion; lymphatic spread to regional lymph nodes; haematogenous spread through veins to lungs
brain; transcoelomic seeding in peritoneal and pleural cavities; implantation along needle tract

answer_html:
Introduction Metastasis is the spread of tumour cells from the primary site to distant, discontinuous sites, where they form secondary tumours. It is the most reliable sign of malignancy and the main cause of cancer deaths. Benign tumours never metastasise.

A. Local invasion Malignant cells break through the basement membrane, infiltrate surrounding tissues, and invade lymphatics and blood vessels – the first step towards metastasis.

B. Routes of metastasis 1. Lymphatic spread

  • Commonest route for carcinomas.
  • Tumour cells enter lymphatics and reach regional lymph nodes (enlarged, hard, painless).
  • Examples: breast cancer → axillary nodes; stomach cancer → left supraclavicular node (Virchow's node); oral cancer → cervical nodes.
  • Sentinel lymph node – first node draining the tumour; biopsy guides surgery.

2. Haematogenous (blood-borne) spread

  • Typical of sarcomas, but also of some carcinomas (kidney, liver, follicular thyroid, lung).
  • Tumour cells invade veins (thin walls) more often than arteries.
  • Common sites of secondaries: lungs and liver (most common), bone, brain, adrenals.
    • Via systemic veins → lungs (e.g., osteosarcoma).
    • Via portal vein → liver (colon, stomach, pancreas cancers).
    • Bone metastases – from prostate, breast, lung, kidney, thyroid.

3. Transcoelomic spread (seeding of body cavities)

  • Tumour cells spread across peritoneal, pleural or pericardial cavities.
  • Examples: ovarian cancer throughout the peritoneum; Krukenberg tumour – stomach cancer spreading to both ovaries; lung cancer to pleura (malignant pleural effusion); ascites.

4. Implantation

  • Direct transfer of tumour cells by surgical instruments, gloves or needle tracts (biopsy), or contact (lip to lip).

C. Steps of the metastatic cascade (brief) Detachment → invasion of extracellular matrix → intravasation → survival in circulation → extravasation → colonisation and angiogenesis at the new site.

D. Grading of cancer

  • Based on the degree of differentiation of tumour cells seen under the microscope.
  • Grade I – well differentiated; Grade II – moderately differentiated; Grade III – poorly differentiated; Grade IV – undifferentiated (anaplastic).
  • Higher grade usually means more aggressive tumour.

E. Staging of cancer

  • Based on the extent of spread, assessed clinically, radiologically and at surgery.
  • TNM system:
    • T – size and local extent of the primary tumour (T0–T4).
    • N – involvement of regional lymph nodes (N0–N3).
    • M – distant metastasis (M0 – absent, M1 – present).
  • TNM combinations give Stages I–IV; Stage IV usually means distant metastasis.
  • Staging is more important than grading for prognosis and treatment planning (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy).

Nursing relevance Examine lymph nodes, report bone pain, cough, jaundice or headache in cancer patients (possible metastasis), care during biopsies, and explain staging and treatment plans in simple words.

Conclusion Malignant tumours spread by lymphatics, blood, body cavities and implantation; grading and staging describe their aggressiveness and extent, guiding treatment and prognosis.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain carcinogenesis and the carcinogenic agents.
answer_html:
Definition Carcinogenesis (oncogenesis) is the multistep process by which normal cells are transformed into cancer cells, through accumulation of genetic damage (mutations). Agents capable of causing cancer are called carcinogens.

A. Molecular basis (brief)

  1. Activation of proto-oncogenes into oncogenes – genes that promote growth become overactive (RAS, MYC, HER2/neu, BCR-ABL).
  2. Inactivation of tumour suppressor genes – genes that restrain growth or trigger apoptosis are lost (p53 – "guardian of the genome", RB, BRCA1/2, APC).
  3. Defects in DNA repair genes and evasion of apoptosis (BCL-2).
  4. Further changes – unlimited replication (telomerase), new blood vessel formation (angiogenesis), invasion, metastasis and escape from immune attack. - Stages: initiation (irreversible DNA damage) → promotion (proliferation of initiated cells by promoters such as hormones, irritation) → progression (malignant behaviour).

B. Carcinogenic agents 1. Chemical carcinogens | Carcinogen | Cancer | |---|---| | Tobacco (smoking, chewing, gutkha, betel quid) – polycyclic hydrocarbons, nitrosamines | Lung, oral cavity (very common in India), larynx, oesophagus, bladder | | Aflatoxin B1 (Aspergillus flavus in mouldy groundnuts and grains) | Liver cancer | | Aromatic amines, aniline dyes (β-naphthylamine) | Urinary bladder | | Asbestos | Mesothelioma, lung cancer | | Benzene | Leukaemia | | Vinyl chloride | Angiosarcoma of liver | | Arsenic (contaminated groundwater) | Skin, lung, bladder | | Alkylating anticancer drugs (cyclophosphamide) | Leukaemia, bladder | | Alcohol | Mouth, oesophagus, liver, breast | | Nitrosamines (preserved foods) | Stomach |

2. Physical carcinogens

  • Ultraviolet rays (sunlight) – skin cancers (basal cell, squamous cell carcinoma, melanoma).
  • Ionising radiation (X-rays, atomic radiation, radon) – leukaemia, thyroid, breast, lung cancers.
  • Chronic irritation/heat – cancer in chronic scars and ulcers (Marjolin's ulcer); Kangri cancer in Kashmir (skin of abdomen from fire-pots).

3. Biological carcinogens

  • Viruses:
    • Human papillomavirus (HPV 16, 18) – cervical cancer, oropharyngeal and anal cancers.
    • Hepatitis B and C viruses – hepatocellular carcinoma.
    • Epstein–Barr virus – Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma.
    • HHV-8 – Kaposi's sarcoma; HTLV-1 – adult T-cell leukaemia; HIV (indirectly).
  • Bacteria: Helicobacter pylori – gastric cancer and MALT lymphoma.
  • Parasites: Schistosoma haematobium – bladder cancer; liver flukes – cholangiocarcinoma.

4. Hormonal and genetic factors

  • Unopposed oestrogen – endometrial and breast cancer.
  • Inherited mutations – BRCA1/2 (breast, ovary), RB (retinoblastoma), APC (colon), Lynch syndrome.

C. Prevention (nursing role)

  • Tobacco and alcohol control – counselling, tobacco cessation centres (National Tobacco Control Programme).
  • Vaccination – HPV vaccine (girls 9–14 years) and hepatitis B vaccine.
  • Healthy diet (fruits, vegetables, fibre), avoiding mouldy grains, weight control, physical activity.
  • Sun protection; occupational safety (PPE, asbestos control).
  • Screening – oral visual inspection, VIA/Pap smear for cervix, clinical breast examination under the national NCD programme.

Conclusion Cancer arises from accumulated genetic damage caused by chemical, physical and biological carcinogens; most cancers in India (tobacco-related, cervical, liver) are largely preventable.

subject: Pathology I
question: Define thrombosis. Explain the factors predisposing to thrombosis and the fate of a thrombus.
answer_html:
Definition Thrombosis is the process of formation of a solid mass (thrombus) from the constituents of blood (platelets, fibrin and trapped red and white cells) within the heart or blood vessels during life. A thrombus differs from a post-mortem clot, which forms after death and is not attached to the vessel wall.

A. Predisposing factors – Virchow's triad 1. Endothelial injury (most important, especially in arteries and heart)

  • Atherosclerosis, myocardial infarction, vasculitis, hypertension, trauma, surgery, smoking, IV cannulas and catheters, bacterial toxins. 2. Abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence)

  • Stasis – immobility, prolonged bed rest, long surgery, long travel, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, varicose veins, aneurysms.

  • Turbulence – arterial bifurcations, ulcerated plaques. 3. Hypercoagulability

  • Acquired – pregnancy and puerperium, oral contraceptives, cancer, nephrotic syndrome, surgery/trauma, obesity, dehydration, smoking, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome, heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.

  • Inherited – factor V Leiden, protein C/S and antithrombin deficiency.

B. Morphology (brief)

  • Arterial thrombi – grey-white, platelet-rich; at sites of endothelial injury (coronary, cerebral arteries).
  • Venous thrombi (phlebothrombosis) – red, rich in RBCs; mostly in deep veins of the legs (DVT).
  • Lines of Zahn – alternating pale (platelets, fibrin) and dark (RBCs) layers – show that the thrombus formed in flowing blood (ante-mortem).

C. Fate of a thrombus

  1. Propagation – the thrombus grows by adding more platelets and fibrin, and may completely block the vessel.
  2. Embolisation – part or whole of the thrombus breaks off and travels in the blood as an embolus – e.g., DVT → pulmonary embolism; heart thrombi → stroke.
  3. Dissolution (resolution) – recent thrombi may be removed by fibrinolysis (plasmin) – the basis of thrombolytic therapy within hours of MI or stroke.
  4. Organisation and recanalisation – older thrombi are invaded by capillaries, fibroblasts and smooth-muscle cells; new channels form through the thrombus, partially restoring blood flow; the thrombus becomes a fibrous mass incorporated into the vessel wall.
  5. Calcification – old venous thrombi may calcify (phleboliths).
  6. Infection (septic thrombus) – bacteria may colonise the thrombus, causing septic emboli and abscesses (e.g., in infective endocarditis).

D. Clinical effects

  • Arterial – ischaemia and infarction (myocardial infarction, stroke, gangrene).
  • Venous – oedema, pain, congestion; pulmonary embolism.

Nursing relevance Prevent DVT by early ambulation, leg exercises, hydration, compression stockings and prophylactic anticoagulants; avoid leg veins for IV cannulas; watch for calf pain, swelling and sudden breathlessness.

Conclusion Thrombosis results from endothelial injury, abnormal flow and hypercoagulability; a thrombus may grow, embolise, dissolve, organise or calcify – and its prevention is a key nursing goal.

subject: Pathology I
question: Define embolism. Describe the types of embolism.
answer_html:
Definition Embolism is the occlusion of a blood vessel by a detached intravascular mass (embolus) – solid, liquid or gaseous – carried by the blood to a site distant from its point of origin.

Types of embolism 1. Thromboembolism (commonest – about 99%)

  • (a) Pulmonary embolism
    • Arises mostly from deep vein thrombosis of the legs and pelvis; travels through the right heart to the pulmonary arteries.
    • Small emboli – may be silent or cause chest pain, cough, haemoptysis (pulmonary infarction).
    • Large emboli ("saddle embolus") at the bifurcation of the pulmonary artery – sudden death due to acute right heart failure.
    • Risk: post-operative, immobile, post-partum, cancer patients.
  • (b) Systemic (arterial) embolism
    • Arises from the left side of the heart – mural thrombi after MI, left atrium in atrial fibrillation, valvular vegetations; or from atherosclerotic plaques.
    • Lodges in arteries of the brain (stroke), lower limbs (gangrene), kidneys, spleen, intestines.
  • Paradoxical embolism – a venous embolus passes to the arterial side through a hole in the heart (patent foramen ovale).

2. Fat embolism

  • Fat globules enter the circulation after fractures of long bones (femur, tibia) or extensive soft-tissue injury/burns.
  • Fat embolism syndrome appears 1–3 days after injury: breathlessness, hypoxia, confusion, petechial rash over chest and axillae, thrombocytopenia.

3. Air (gas) embolism

  • Venous air embolism – air entering through IV lines, central venous catheters (insertion/removal), neck and chest surgery, criminal abortion; about 100 ml of air or more may be fatal (frothy blood blocks the heart).
  • Decompression sickness (caisson disease, "the bends") – divers or tunnel workers ascending rapidly; dissolved nitrogen forms bubbles in tissues and vessels → joint pain, breathlessness, neurological signs.

4. Amniotic fluid embolism

  • A rare, often fatal complication of labour or immediately after delivery; amniotic fluid with fetal cells enters maternal circulation → sudden breathlessness, cyanosis, shock, convulsions and DIC (bleeding).

5. Other emboli

  • Tumour emboli (spread of cancer), septic emboli (infective endocarditis), atheromatous (cholesterol) emboli, foreign bodies (catheter fragments, talc in drug users), parasites.

Effects Depend on size of embolus, site, collateral circulation and the general condition of the patient – from no effect to infarction or sudden death.

Nursing relevance

  • DVT prevention; early mobilisation after surgery and delivery.
  • Prime IV tubing fully, tighten connections, place patients flat/Trendelenburg during central line removal and ask them to perform Valsalva (as per policy).
  • Immobilise fractures properly; monitor oxygen saturation and mental status after long-bone fractures.

Conclusion Most emboli are detached thrombi, but fat, air and amniotic fluid emboli also occur; many are preventable by good nursing care.

subject: Pathology I
question: Define infarction. Describe the types, causes and morphology of infarcts.
answer_html:
Definition An infarct is an area of ischaemic necrosis caused by occlusion of the arterial supply or venous drainage of a tissue; the process is called infarction. Infarction of the heart and brain are among the leading causes of death in India.

1. Causes

  • Arterial thrombosis (over atherosclerotic plaques) and embolism – most common.
  • Others – vasospasm, external compression (tumour), torsion of vessels (testis, ovary), haemorrhage into a plaque, venous thrombosis (in organs with single venous outflow).

2. Types (a) According to colour | Type | Features | Examples | |---|---|---| | White (pale, anaemic) infarcts | Arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation; little bleeding into the area | Heart, kidney, spleen | | Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts | Venous occlusion, loose tissues, organs with dual blood supply, reperfusion of dead tissue | Lungs, intestine, ovary/testis (torsion), brain after reperfusion | (b) According to infection

  • Bland (sterile) and septic (infected – e.g., emboli from infective endocarditis → abscess).

3. Morphology

  • Gross: usually wedge-shaped, with the apex at the occluded vessel and the base at the organ surface (kidney, spleen, lung); margins well defined, with a red inflammatory border initially; later replaced by a pale, depressed scar.
  • Microscopy: coagulative necrosis (ghost outlines) in most organs; liquefactive necrosis in the brain; inflammatory cells at the margin; granulation tissue and fibrosis later.

4. Factors influencing the development of an infarct

  1. Nature of blood supply – organs with dual supply (lungs, liver) or rich collaterals resist infarction; end-arterial organs (kidney, spleen) infarct easily.
  2. Rate of occlusion – slow occlusion allows collaterals to develop.
  3. Vulnerability of tissue to hypoxia – neurons die in 3–5 minutes, myocardium in 20–30 minutes, fibroblasts survive for hours.
  4. Oxygen content of blood – anaemia, heart failure and hypoxia worsen infarction.

5. Important examples

  • Myocardial infarction – coronary thrombosis; arrhythmias, heart failure, rupture.
  • Cerebral infarction (ischaemic stroke) – paralysis, aphasia.
  • Pulmonary infarction – haemoptysis, pleuritic chest pain.
  • Renal and splenic infarcts – flank or left upper quadrant pain, haematuria.
  • Intestinal (mesenteric) infarction – severe pain, bloody stools, gangrene of bowel – surgical emergency.

Nursing relevance Recognise warning signs (chest pain, sudden weakness, severe abdominal pain), ensure early reperfusion (thrombolysis/angioplasty within the "golden hours"), oxygen and monitoring, and prevention through control of risk factors.

Conclusion Infarcts are areas of ischaemic necrosis; their type and size depend on the blood supply, speed of occlusion and tissue sensitivity – early treatment limits the damage.

subject: Pathology I
question: Write a note on septic shock.
answer_html:
Introduction Shock is a state of systemic hypoperfusion caused by reduced cardiac output or reduced effective circulating blood volume, leading to hypotension, impaired tissue perfusion and cellular hypoxia. Septic shock is the commonest cause of death in intensive care units.

1. Definitions (Sepsis-3)

  • Sepsis – life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
  • Septic shock – sepsis with circulatory and metabolic abnormalities severe enough to need vasopressors to maintain mean arterial pressure ≥65 mmHg and with serum lactate >2 mmol/l despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

2. Causes

  • Gram-negative bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, meningococcus) – endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide).
  • Gram-positive bacteria (S. aureus, streptococci), fungi (Candida).
  • Common sources – pneumonia, urinary tract infection, intra-abdominal infection, wound and line infections; risk is higher in elderly, diabetics, immunocompromised patients and those with invasive devices.

3. Pathogenesis

  1. Microbial products (endotoxin, peptidoglycan) are recognised by Toll-like receptors on macrophages, neutrophils and endothelium.
  2. Massive release of cytokines – TNF, IL-1, IL-6 ("cytokine storm"), activation of complement and coagulation.
  3. Systemic vasodilation (nitric oxide) → hypotension and maldistribution of blood flow.
  4. Increased vascular permeability → loss of fluid into tissues, oedema.
  5. Endothelial activation and DIC – microthrombi, consumption of clotting factors → bleeding.
  6. Myocardial depression, metabolic changes (insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, lactic acidosis), immune suppression.
  7. Result: multi-organ dysfunction syndrome (MODS).

4. Stages of shock

  • Non-progressive (compensated) – reflexes (sympathetic activation, renin–angiotensin system, ADH) maintain BP; tachycardia, vasoconstriction (in septic shock skin may be warm and flushed early).
  • Progressive – tissue hypoperfusion, anaerobic metabolism, lactic acidosis, confusion, oliguria, worsening hypotension.
  • Irreversible – severe cell damage, lysosomal enzyme release, failure of heart, kidneys and other organs; death despite treatment.

5. Morphological changes in organs

  • Lungs – diffuse alveolar damage (ARDS, "shock lung").
  • Kidneys – acute tubular necrosis (acute kidney injury).
  • Adrenals – lipid depletion, haemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen syndrome in meningococcal sepsis).
  • Heart – contraction-band necrosis; liver – fatty change, central necrosis; brain – ischaemic encephalopathy; GI – mucosal haemorrhages.

6. Laboratory findings Leukocytosis or leukopenia, raised lactate, positive blood cultures, raised CRP/procalcitonin, low platelets and prolonged PT/aPTT (DIC), rising creatinine and bilirubin.

7. Management principles and nursing role

  • Early recognition (fever or hypothermia, tachycardia, tachypnoea, hypotension, altered sensorium, oliguria).
  • "Sepsis bundle" – blood cultures before antibiotics, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, IV crystalloids (30 ml/kg), measure lactate, vasopressors (noradrenaline) for persistent hypotension.
  • Source control (drain abscess, remove infected line).
  • Monitor vital signs, urine output, consciousness, SpO₂; infection control.

Conclusion Septic shock results from an uncontrolled inflammatory response to infection, causing vasodilation, leaky vessels, clotting abnormalities and multi-organ failure; early recognition and the sepsis bundle save lives.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain hyperaemia and congestion. Describe the chronic venous congestion of lung and liver.
answer_html:
Introduction Disturbances of blood flow are common in clinical practice. Hyperaemia and congestion both mean an increased volume of blood in a tissue, but they differ in mechanism and effects.

1. Hyperaemia (active)

  • Active process due to arteriolar dilation → increased inflow of blood.
  • Tissue appears red and warm (oxygenated blood).
  • Examples: acute inflammation, exercising muscle, blushing, fever.

2. Congestion (passive)

  • Passive process due to impaired venous outflow of blood.
  • Tissue appears bluish-red (cyanosed) because of deoxygenated blood; may be associated with oedema.
  • Systemic causes: heart failure (left-sided → lungs; right-sided → liver, spleen, legs).
  • Local causes: venous obstruction (DVT, tight bandage, tumour compression).
  • May be acute or chronic.

3. Chronic venous congestion (CVC) of the lungs

  • Cause: left ventricular failure and mitral stenosis (common in rheumatic heart disease in India).
  • Gross: lungs are heavy, firm and brown – "brown induration".
  • Microscopy:
    • Alveolar capillaries are dilated and engorged.
    • Alveolar walls thickened and fibrosed.
    • Microhaemorrhages into alveoli; macrophages engulf red cells and contain brown haemosiderin pigment – called "heart failure cells" (can be seen in sputum).
  • Clinical: breathlessness, orthopnoea, cough, crepitations, rusty sputum.

4. Chronic venous congestion of the liver

  • Cause: right ventricular failure (e.g., cor pulmonale, tricuspid valve disease, constrictive pericarditis).
  • Gross: liver enlarged, tender; cut surface shows dark red congested central areas alternating with pale yellow fatty peripheral areas – "nutmeg liver".
  • Microscopy: centrilobular congestion and haemorrhage, centrilobular necrosis (hypoxia), fatty change in the periphery; long-standing cases develop fibrosis – cardiac cirrhosis (cardiac sclerosis).
  • Clinical: tender hepatomegaly, raised JVP, ascites, mild jaundice.

5. Related terms – haemorrhage

  • Petechiae (1–2 mm), purpura (≥3 mm), ecchymoses (1–2 cm, bruises), haematoma (collection of blood in tissue).
  • Bleeding into cavities – haemothorax, haemopericardium, haemoperitoneum, haemarthrosis.

Nursing relevance Propped-up position and oxygen for pulmonary congestion; daily weight, fluid and salt restriction in heart failure; observation of sputum, liver tenderness and oedema.

6. Comparison | Hyperaemia | Congestion | |---|---| | Active – increased arterial inflow | Passive – reduced venous outflow | | Bright red, warm | Bluish-red, cool | | Short-lived | May be chronic, with oedema and fibrosis |

Conclusion Hyperaemia is active and protective; congestion is passive and, when chronic, damages lungs (brown induration) and liver (nutmeg liver).

subject: Pathology I
question: Define ischaemia.
answer_html:
Ischaemia is a reduction or complete cessation of blood supply to a tissue or organ relative to its needs, resulting in lack of oxygen (hypoxia), reduced supply of nutrients and accumulation of waste products.

Causes: atherosclerosis, thrombosis, embolism, vasospasm, external compression (tight plaster, tourniquet), hypotension/shock. Effects: reversible injury and pain (e.g., angina), atrophy (chronic ischaemia), or infarction (necrosis) if severe and prolonged (e.g., myocardial infarction, stroke). Ischaemia is more harmful than hypoxia alone because waste products are not removed.

subject: Pathology I
question: List any two types of necrosis with one example each.
answer_html:
Types of necrosis (any two)

  1. Coagulative necrosis – myocardial infarction, renal and splenic infarcts.
  2. Liquefactive necrosis – abscess, brain infarct.
  3. Caseous necrosis – tuberculosis.
  4. Fat necrosis – acute pancreatitis, traumatic fat necrosis of breast.
  5. Fibrinoid necrosis – vasculitis, malignant hypertension.
  6. Gangrenous necrosis – diabetic foot (dry/wet gangrene).

Definition: necrosis is the death of a group of cells or tissue in a living body due to irreversible injury, followed by inflammation. The commonest form is coagulative necrosis, seen in infarcts of solid organs (except the brain).

subject: Pathology I
question: Define shock and list any two types.
answer_html:
Shock is a life-threatening state of circulatory failure in which reduced cardiac output or reduced effective circulating blood volume causes hypotension, inadequate tissue perfusion and cellular hypoxia, leading to organ dysfunction if uncorrected.

Types (any two)

  1. Hypovolaemic shock – haemorrhage, burns, severe vomiting/diarrhoea.
  2. Cardiogenic shock – myocardial infarction, arrhythmias.
  3. Septic shock – severe infection (endotoxins, cytokines).
  4. Anaphylactic shock – severe allergy.
  5. Neurogenic shock – spinal cord injury; obstructive shock – pulmonary embolism, tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade.

Early signs: tachycardia, cold clammy skin (warm in early septic shock), falling BP, oliguria, restlessness.

subject: Pathology I
question: Give the differences between benign and malignant tumours.
answer_html:
Feature Benign Malignant
Growth rate Slow Rapid
Mode of growth Expansile, encapsulated Infiltrative, not encapsulated
Differentiation Well differentiated Poor to anaplastic
Metastasis Absent Present
Recurrence Rare Common
Nuclei and mitoses Normal, few Pleomorphic, many abnormal mitoses
Effect on host Local pressure only Cachexia, can be fatal
Necrosis and haemorrhage Rare Common
Capsule Usually present Absent
Example Lipoma, fibroadenoma Carcinoma, sarcoma

Key point: invasion and metastasis are the most reliable features of malignancy; the final diagnosis is made by histopathology (biopsy).

subject: Pathology I
question: Define metaplasia. Give examples.
answer_html:
Metaplasia is a reversible change in which one adult (fully differentiated) cell type is replaced by another adult cell type, usually one better able to withstand a chronic stress.

Examples

  1. Squamous metaplasia of the ciliated columnar epithelium of bronchi in chronic smokers (and in vitamin A deficiency).
  2. Barrett's oesophagus – squamous epithelium of lower oesophagus replaced by intestinal-type columnar epithelium in chronic acid reflux.
  3. Squamous metaplasia in the cervix (transformation zone) and bladder (stones, schistosomiasis).

Significance: loss of protective function; persistent stimulus may lead to dysplasia and cancer.

subject: Pathology I
question: What is gangrene? Mention its types.
answer_html:
Gangrene is necrosis of tissue (usually a limb or bowel) with superadded putrefaction (decomposition by bacteria), giving a black or green colour and foul smell.

Types

  1. Dry gangrene – slow arterial occlusion (atherosclerosis, diabetes, Buerger's disease, frostbite); part becomes dry, shrunken, black ("mummified") with a clear line of demarcation; spreads slowly.
  2. Wet gangrene – arterial plus venous obstruction in moist tissues (strangulated bowel, diabetic foot, bedsores); swollen, soft, foul-smelling, no clear demarcation; spreads fast and causes septicaemia.
  3. Gas gangrene – infection of dead muscle by Clostridium perfringens; gas in tissues (crepitus), severe toxaemia – emergency.

subject: Pathology I
question: What is an abscess?
answer_html:
An abscess is a localised collection of pus within a tissue cavity formed by liquefactive necrosis, surrounded by a wall of granulation tissue (pyogenic membrane) and later fibrous tissue.

Pus consists of dead and living neutrophils, necrotic tissue, bacteria and inflammatory exudate. Causes: pyogenic bacteria – most commonly Staphylococcus aureus; amoebae (amoebic liver abscess). Sites: skin (boil), breast, liver, lung, brain, perianal region, tooth. Treatment: incision and drainage ("where there is pus, let it out") with antibiotics; aseptic dressing.

Untreated abscesses may rupture, form sinuses or spread to cause septicaemia.

subject: Pathology I
question: Define oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes with examples.
answer_html:
Oncogenes – mutated or overactive forms of normal growth-promoting genes (proto-oncogenes) that drive uncontrolled cell proliferation; one altered copy is enough (dominant action).

  • Examples: RAS (pancreas, colon, lung cancers), MYC (Burkitt's lymphoma), HER2/neu (breast cancer – target of trastuzumab), BCR-ABL (chronic myeloid leukaemia – target of imatinib).

Tumour suppressor genes – normal genes that restrain cell growth, repair DNA or trigger apoptosis; cancer develops when both copies are lost ("two-hit").

  • Examples: p53 ("guardian of the genome" – mutated in about half of all cancers), RB (retinoblastoma), BRCA1/BRCA2 (breast and ovarian cancer), APC (colon cancer).

subject: Pathology I
question: Define hypokalaemia and mention its causes and effects.
answer_html:
Hypokalaemia is a serum potassium level below 3.5 mEq/l.

Causes

  • GI losses – vomiting, diarrhoea, nasogastric aspiration, laxative abuse.
  • Renal losses – diuretics (furosemide, thiazides), hyperaldosteronism, treatment of DKA.
  • Shift into cells – insulin, salbutamol, alkalosis; poor intake.

Effects

  • Muscle weakness, cramps, paralytic ileus, constipation.
  • ECG changes – flat T waves, U waves, arrhythmias; increases digoxin toxicity.

Treatment: oral or IV potassium chloride – never as an IV push; dilute and infuse slowly with a pump.

Normal serum potassium is 3.5–5.0 mEq/l; monitor it in patients on diuretics, digoxin and IV fluids.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the pathological changes in pulmonary tuberculosis and their clinical manifestations.

diagram.caption: Lesions of pulmonary tuberculosis
labels: primary Ghon complex (subpleural focus and hilar node)

answer_html:
Introduction Pulmonary tuberculosis is a chronic granulomatous infection of the lungs caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, spread by droplet nuclei. The tissue damage is mainly due to the body's cell-mediated (type IV) hypersensitivity reaction rather than toxins.

A. Primary pulmonary tuberculosis (first infection, usually children)

  1. Ghon focus – a 1–1.5 cm grey-white area of consolidation, subpleural, in the lower part of the upper lobe or upper part of the lower lobe.
  2. Bacilli drain to hilar lymph nodes, which enlarge and caseate.
  3. Ghon focus + lymphangitis + hilar lymphadenitis = primary (Ghon) complex.
  4. Microscopy: caseating granulomas – central caseous necrosis, surrounded by epithelioid cells, Langhans giant cells, lymphocytes and fibroblasts.
  5. Outcome: in most people the lesion heals by fibrosis and calcification (Ranke complex); bacilli may remain dormant. In infants, malnourished or HIV-positive persons it may progress – progressive primary TB, tuberculous bronchopneumonia, miliary TB, TB meningitis.
  6. Manifestations: often asymptomatic, or mild fever, cough, failure to thrive; positive Mantoux test.

B. Secondary (post-primary, reactivation) tuberculosis (adults)

  1. Occurs by reactivation of dormant bacilli (or reinfection) when immunity falls (HIV, diabetes, malnutrition, steroids, alcohol).
  2. Begins at the apex of one or both lungs (high oxygen tension) – Assmann/Simon foci.
  3. Because the body is already sensitised, there is extensive caseation.
  4. Caseous material liquefies and drains into a bronchus → cavity formation – cavities contain millions of bacilli (patient becomes highly infectious).
  5. Erosion of blood vessels (sometimes a Rasmussen aneurysm in the cavity wall) → haemoptysis.
  6. Spread: through bronchi (tuberculous bronchopneumonia), to larynx and intestines (swallowed sputum), to pleura (effusion, empyema), through blood (miliary TB – millet-seed lesions in lungs, liver, spleen, kidneys, meninges).
  7. Healing: fibrosis, calcification, retraction of lung, bronchiectasis.

C. Clinical manifestations (correlation with pathology) | Pathology | Manifestation | |---|---| | Cytokine release (TNF, IL-1) | Evening fever, night sweats, weight loss, loss of appetite, fatigue | | Caseation and cavitation | Cough with sputum for more than 2 weeks | | Erosion of vessels | Haemoptysis (blood in sputum) | | Pleural involvement | Pleuritic chest pain, pleural effusion, breathlessness | | Fibrosis | Breathlessness, tracheal deviation, crepitations | | Miliary spread | High fever, enlarged liver/spleen, choroid tubercles, meningitis |

D. Complications Massive haemoptysis, pleural effusion, empyema, pneumothorax, bronchiectasis, cor pulmonale, aspergilloma in old cavities, amyloidosis, laryngeal and intestinal TB.

E. Diagnosis (brief) Sputum smear (ZN), CBNAAT/Truenat, culture, chest X-ray (upper-lobe infiltrates, cavities), histopathology of biopsy.

Nursing relevance Airborne infection control, sputum collection and disposal, adherence to treatment, nutrition, monitoring for haemoptysis.

Conclusion Primary TB forms the Ghon complex and usually heals; secondary TB causes apical caseation and cavities, producing cough, fever, weight loss and haemoptysis.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the clinical features and types of emphysema.

diagram.caption: Types of emphysema according to the part of the acinus involved
labels: normal acinus; centriacinar – respiratory bronchioles enlarged; panacinar – whole acinus enlarged; paraseptal – distal acinus near pleura with bullae

answer_html:
Definition Emphysema is a condition characterised by permanent enlargement of the airspaces distal to the terminal bronchioles, accompanied by destruction of their walls, without obvious fibrosis. Together with chronic bronchitis it forms chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), a leading cause of death in India (tobacco smoke and biomass fuel smoke).

A. Pathogenesis (brief)

  1. Protease–antiprotease imbalance – tobacco smoke attracts neutrophils and macrophages, which release elastase and other proteases that destroy alveolar walls; normally α1-antitrypsin inhibits elastase. Smoke also inactivates α1-antitrypsin.
  2. Oxidant–antioxidant imbalance – free radicals in smoke damage tissue.
  3. Inherited α1-antitrypsin deficiency – emphysema in young non-smokers.
  4. Loss of elastic recoil → small airways collapse during expiration → air trapping.

B. Types of emphysema (based on the part of the acinus involved) | Type | Part involved | Distribution | Association | |---|---|---|---| | Centriacinar (centrilobular) | Respiratory bronchioles (central part); distal alveoli spared | Upper lobes, apical segments | Smokers – commonest type (over 95%) | | Panacinar (panlobular) | Entire acinus uniformly enlarged | Lower lobes, bases | α1-antitrypsin deficiency | | Paraseptal (distal acinar) | Distal part of acinus, along pleura and septa | Upper lobes, near fibrosis | Spontaneous pneumothorax in young adults (bullae rupture) | | Irregular | Acinus irregularly involved | With scars | Clinically insignificant | Other terms: bullous emphysema (large air spaces – bullae), compensatory emphysema (after lung removal), senile emphysema (ageing), interstitial emphysema (air in the interstitium after trauma or ventilation).

C. Morphology

  • Gross: voluminous, pale lungs that overlap the heart; bullae may be seen.
  • Microscopy: enlarged airspaces, destroyed alveolar septa, loss of capillary bed, thinned walls.

D. Clinical features

  1. Progressive breathlessness (dyspnoea) – first on exertion, later at rest; the main symptom.
  2. Cough – mild, with little sputum (unless with chronic bronchitis).
  3. Weight loss, fatigue.
  4. "Pink puffer" appearance – patient is thin, breathes through pursed lips, uses accessory muscles, sits leaning forward (tripod position), with prolonged expiration; oxygenation relatively maintained until late.
  5. Barrel-shaped chest (increased antero-posterior diameter), hyper-resonant percussion, diminished breath sounds, reduced cardiac dullness.
  6. Investigations: chest X-ray – hyperinflation, flattened diaphragm, narrow heart, bullae; spirometry – reduced FEV₁/FVC (obstruction), increased total lung capacity and residual volume, reduced diffusing capacity.
  7. Complications: respiratory failure, cor pulmonale (right heart failure), pneumothorax, recurrent infections, polycythaemia.

Nursing relevance Smoking cessation, avoidance of biomass smoke, pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing exercises, controlled oxygen therapy, vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), nutrition.

Conclusion Emphysema results from destruction of alveolar walls by proteases; centriacinar emphysema in smokers is the commonest type, causing progressive breathlessness and hyperinflated lungs.

subject: Pathology I
question: Differentiate between lobar pneumonia and bronchopneumonia. Describe the stages of lobar pneumonia.

diagram.caption: Stages of lobar pneumonia
labels: congestion – engorged capillaries and fluid; red hepatisation – neutrophils
fibrin; grey hepatisation – fibrin and disintegrating cells; resolution – exudate cleared by macrophages

answer_html:
Definition Pneumonia is an acute inflammation of the lung parenchyma (alveoli) caused usually by infection, in which the alveoli fill with exudate (consolidation). Morphologically it is classified into lobar pneumonia and bronchopneumonia.

A. Differences | Feature | Lobar pneumonia | Bronchopneumonia | |---|---|---| | Distribution | Whole lobe (or large part) uniformly consolidated | Patchy consolidation around bronchioles | | Lobes involved | Usually one lobe | Multiple lobes, often bilateral, lower lobes | | Common organisms | Streptococcus pneumoniae (90%), Klebsiella | S. aureus, H. influenzae, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, streptococci | | Age/host | Healthy young adults | Infants, elderly, debilitated, post-operative, bedridden patients | | Onset | Sudden – high fever, rigors, pleuritic pain, rusty sputum | Gradual, often following another illness | | Pleura | Fibrinous pleurisy common | Less common | | Stages | Distinct stages | No distinct stages | | Prognosis | Good with treatment | More serious in the elderly and infants |

B. Stages of lobar pneumonia (classical, untreated) 1. Stage of congestion (first 1–2 days)

  • Lobe is heavy, red and boggy.
  • Alveolar capillaries are engorged; alveoli contain oedema fluid with a few neutrophils and many bacteria.

2. Stage of red hepatisation (days 2–4)

  • Lobe becomes red, firm and liver-like (hepatisation) – airless.
  • Alveoli are filled with neutrophils, red blood cells and fibrin.
  • Overlying pleura shows fibrinous exudate (pleurisy).
  • Clinically – high fever, rusty sputum (RBCs), bronchial breath sounds.

3. Stage of grey hepatisation (days 4–8)

  • Lobe becomes greyish-brown, dry and firm.
  • Red cells disintegrate; fibrin and neutrophils persist.

4. Stage of resolution (from day 8–9)

  • Exudate is digested by enzymes, removed by macrophages, coughed up or absorbed; lung architecture is restored.
  • With early antibiotics, this sequence is shortened.

C. Complications Lung abscess, empyema, fibrous pleural adhesions, organisation of exudate (carnification), spread to blood – bacteraemia, meningitis, endocarditis, arthritis.

Nursing relevance Positioning, oxygen, encouragement of coughing and deep breathing, fluids, antibiotics on time, sputum culture before antibiotics, vaccination (pneumococcal, influenza) for the elderly.

D. Other forms of pneumonia (brief)

  • Atypical (interstitial) pneumonia – Mycoplasma, viruses (influenza, SARS-CoV-2); inflammation mainly in alveolar walls, little exudate in alveoli; dry cough, patchy X-ray shadows.
  • Aspiration pneumonia – in unconscious, alcoholic or stroke patients; right lower lobe commonly; often abscess-forming.
  • Hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia – Gram-negative organisms; prevented by head-end elevation and oral care.

Conclusion Lobar pneumonia involves an entire lobe in four classic stages, while bronchopneumonia is patchy and commoner in the very young, old and debilitated.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the pathology of myocardial infarction.
answer_html:
Definition Myocardial infarction (MI) is necrosis of heart muscle due to prolonged ischaemia, usually caused by sudden occlusion of a coronary artery by a thrombus over a ruptured atherosclerotic plaque. It is a leading cause of death in India, often at younger ages than in Western countries.

1. Pathogenesis

  1. Atherosclerotic plaque in a coronary artery suddenly ruptures or erodes.
  2. Platelets adhere and aggregate; thrombus forms and occludes the artery.
  3. Myocardium supplied by the artery becomes ischaemic – irreversible injury begins after 20–40 minutes; most damage occurs within the first 3–6 hours ("time is muscle").
  4. Less common causes – coronary spasm, embolism, vasculitis.

2. Types

  • Transmural infarct – involves the full thickness of the wall (usually ST-elevation MI).
  • Subendocardial infarct – inner third of the wall (non-ST-elevation MI).

3. Sites (artery involved)

  • Left anterior descending artery (40–50%) – anterior wall of left ventricle, apex, anterior two-thirds of septum.
  • Right coronary artery (30–40%) – inferior/posterior wall, posterior septum.
  • Left circumflex artery (15–20%) – lateral wall.

4. Morphological changes (time course) | Time | Gross | Microscopy | |---|---|---| | 0–12 hours | Not visible (special stains show the area) | Wavy fibres, early coagulative necrosis | | 12–24 hours | Dark mottling | Coagulative necrosis, contraction bands, neutrophils begin | | 1–3 days | Yellow-tan centre | Necrosis with dense neutrophil infiltrate | | 3–7 days | Soft yellow centre with red border | Macrophages remove dead cells – wall weakest (risk of rupture) | | 7–10 days | Yellow with red margins | Granulation tissue at margins | | 2–8 weeks | Grey-white | Collagen deposition | | After 2 months | Firm grey-white scar | Dense fibrous scar |

5. Complications

  1. Arrhythmias – ventricular fibrillation (commonest cause of sudden death), heart block.
  2. Left ventricular failure and cardiogenic shock.
  3. Rupture – of free wall (cardiac tamponade), interventricular septum or papillary muscle (acute mitral regurgitation) – usually days 3–7.
  4. Pericarditis – early fibrinous; later autoimmune (Dressler's syndrome, weeks after).
  5. Mural thrombus and embolism (stroke).
  6. Ventricular aneurysm.
  7. Extension and re-infarction.

6. Laboratory findings Rise in cardiac troponins (most specific) and CK-MB; ECG changes (ST elevation, Q waves); leukocytosis, raised ESR.

Nursing relevance Early recognition of chest pain, rapid ECG and transfer for reperfusion, rest in the first days (weakest period of the wall), cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias, and risk-factor modification.

Conclusion MI is coagulative necrosis of the myocardium following coronary thrombosis; it evolves from neutrophil infiltration to scar over weeks, with arrhythmias and pump failure as the main dangers.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the pathogenesis and pathological changes of rheumatic heart disease.

diagram.caption: Aschoff body and fish-mouth mitral stenosis in rheumatic heart disease
labels: fused mitral valve leaflets with narrow opening

answer_html:
Introduction Rheumatic fever (RF) is an acute, immunologically mediated, multisystem inflammatory disease that follows group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis. Repeated attacks damage the heart valves, causing chronic rheumatic heart disease (RHD) – still common in children and young adults in India.

1. Pathogenesis

  1. Streptococcal sore throat (not skin infection) in a genetically susceptible child (5–15 years).
  2. After a latent period of 2–3 weeks, the body forms antibodies and T cells against streptococcal antigens (especially M protein).
  3. These cross-react with heart tissues (myosin, valve glycoproteins), joints, skin and brain – molecular mimicry (type II hypersensitivity and cell-mediated injury).
  4. Repeated infections cause repeated attacks and progressive valve damage.

2. Acute rheumatic fever – pathology ("pancarditis")

  • Aschoff bodies – pathognomonic lesions: foci of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by lymphocytes, plasma cells and Anitschkow cells ("caterpillar cells" with wavy chromatin) and Aschoff giant cells.
  • Pericarditis – fibrinous ("bread and butter" appearance).
  • Myocarditis – Aschoff bodies in interstitial tissue; may cause heart failure.
  • Endocarditis (valvulitis) – small, warty vegetations (verrucae) along the lines of closure of the mitral and aortic valves; MacCallum's plaque in the left atrium.
  • Extra-cardiac: migratory polyarthritis of large joints (heals without deformity), subcutaneous nodules, erythema marginatum, Sydenham's chorea.
  • Diagnosis by Jones criteria with evidence of recent streptococcal infection (raised ASO titre).

3. Chronic rheumatic heart disease

  • Healing by fibrosis leads to thickening, calcification and fusion of valve commissures, thickened, shortened and fused chordae tendineae.
  • Mitral valve is involved most often (about 65–70%), then mitral + aortic; tricuspid rarely; pulmonary almost never.
  • Mitral stenosis – "fish-mouth" or "buttonhole" orifice.
  • Also mitral regurgitation, aortic stenosis/regurgitation.

4. Complications Left atrial enlargement, atrial fibrillation, left atrial thrombus and systemic embolism (stroke), pulmonary congestion and hypertension, congestive heart failure, infective endocarditis on damaged valves.

5. Prevention and nursing relevance

  • Primary prevention – prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat with penicillin (10 days oral or single benzathine penicillin injection).
  • Secondary prevention – benzathine penicillin 1.2 million units IM every 3 weeks (as per Indian guidelines) for years after an attack.
  • Rest during acute carditis, aspirin/steroids as ordered, dental hygiene and antibiotic prophylaxis before dental procedures where indicated.

Conclusion RHD is an immunological sequel of streptococcal sore throat; Aschoff bodies mark the acute stage, and fibrotic, fused valves – especially mitral stenosis – mark the chronic stage. Penicillin prophylaxis prevents it.

subject: Pathology I
question: Write a note on infective endocarditis.
answer_html:
Definition Infective endocarditis (IE) is an infection of the endocardium, usually of the heart valves, by microorganisms (mainly bacteria), with formation of friable, bulky vegetations containing organisms, fibrin and platelets.

1. Types | Feature | Acute IE | Subacute IE | |---|---|---| | Organism | Highly virulent – Staphylococcus aureus | Low virulence – viridans streptococci, enterococci | | Valve | Often normal valves; tricuspid in IV drug users | Previously damaged valves (RHD, congenital heart disease, prosthetic valves) | | Course | Rapid, destructive; death in days–weeks | Slow, weeks–months | | Source | Skin infections, IV lines, drug injection | Dental procedures, poor oral hygiene, GI/urinary procedures |

2. Predisposing factors

  • Rheumatic heart disease (most common in India), congenital heart defects (VSD, PDA, bicuspid aortic valve), prosthetic heart valves, degenerative valve disease.
  • Bacteraemia – dental extraction, poor dental hygiene, urinary catheterisation, central venous catheters, haemodialysis, IV drug abuse.
  • Immunosuppression, diabetes.

3. Pathogenesis and morphology

  • Damaged endothelium → platelet–fibrin deposits → colonised by circulating bacteria → bacteria multiply protected from defences.
  • Vegetations – large, friable, irregular masses on valve cusps (mitral and aortic most often); may perforate or destroy valves, extend into the myocardium (ring abscess).
  • Fragments break off → septic emboli.

4. Clinical features

  • Fever (most common), weakness, weight loss, anaemia, clubbing, splenomegaly.
  • New or changing heart murmur; heart failure due to valve destruction.
  • Embolic phenomena – stroke, infarcts of spleen, kidney, limbs; splinter haemorrhages under nails, Janeway lesions (painless spots on palms/soles), Osler's nodes (painful nodules on fingertips), Roth spots (retina); glomerulonephritis (haematuria).

5. Diagnosis

  • Blood cultures – at least three sets from different sites before antibiotics (most important).
  • Echocardiography (transthoracic/transoesophageal) to see vegetations.
  • Modified Duke criteria; raised ESR/CRP, anaemia, haematuria.

6. Complications and treatment (brief) Heart failure, emboli, mycotic aneurysms, abscesses, kidney failure; treated with prolonged IV bactericidal antibiotics (4–6 weeks) and surgery for valve destruction.

Nursing relevance Strict asepsis with IV lines, proper collection of blood cultures, dental hygiene education for patients with valve disease, monitoring temperature and signs of embolism.

Prevention Good oral and dental hygiene in patients with valve disease, antibiotic prophylaxis before selected dental procedures in high-risk patients (prosthetic valves, previous endocarditis) as per guidelines, aseptic care of central lines, and treatment of skin infections.

Conclusion Infective endocarditis is a serious infection of damaged or normal valves producing vegetations, emboli and valve destruction; early blood cultures and prolonged antibiotics are lifesaving.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the pathology of peptic ulcer.
answer_html:
Definition A peptic ulcer is a breach in the mucosa of the alimentary tract extending through the muscularis mucosae into the submucosa or deeper, in areas exposed to acid–pepsin. (An erosion is a superficial defect that does not cross the muscularis mucosae.)

1. Sites

  • First part of the duodenum (commonest – about four times more common than gastric ulcer).
  • Stomach – usually the lesser curvature near the antrum.
  • Lower oesophagus (reflux), stoma of gastrojejunostomy, Meckel's diverticulum (ectopic gastric mucosa).

2. Pathogenesis – imbalance between aggressive and protective factors Aggressive factors

  • Helicobacter pylori infection (most important – found in most duodenal and many gastric ulcers).
  • NSAIDs and aspirin – inhibit prostaglandins (protective).
  • Excess acid – Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrin-secreting tumour).

  • Smoking, alcohol, corticosteroids with NSAIDs, stress (burns – Curling's ulcer; head injury – Cushing's ulcer). Defensive factors (weakened)

  • Mucus–bicarbonate barrier, mucosal blood flow, prostaglandins, epithelial renewal.

  • Genetic factors (blood group O), chronic diseases (cirrhosis, chronic lung disease).

3. Morphology

  • Gross: usually single, round to oval, sharply punched-out ulcer, 1–4 cm, with straight walls, smooth clean base, edges flat (not raised); mucosal folds radiate from the ulcer.
  • Microscopy – four zones from the surface:
    1. Thin layer of necrotic debris and fibrin.
    2. Non-specific inflammatory cells (neutrophils).
    3. Granulation tissue.
    4. Fibrous scar at the base, with thickened arteries.

4. Clinical features (brief) Epigastric burning pain – duodenal ulcer pain relieved by food and occurring at night; gastric ulcer pain worsened by food; nausea, weight loss.

5. Complications

  1. Bleeding – commonest (haematemesis, malaena, anaemia).
  2. Perforation – sudden severe pain, peritonitis (emergency).
  3. Gastric outlet obstruction – due to scarring near the pylorus (projectile vomiting).
  4. Penetration into pancreas or liver.
  5. Malignant change – rare in gastric ulcers; never in duodenal ulcers.

6. Benign versus malignant gastric ulcer (brief) Benign – regular, punched-out with flat margins; malignant – irregular, heaped-up everted edges, necrotic base – biopsy is essential.

Nursing relevance Avoid NSAIDs and smoking, complete H. pylori therapy, watch for black stools and haematemesis, recognise signs of perforation.

Conclusion Peptic ulcer results from acid–pepsin injury when defences are weakened, most often due to H. pylori and NSAIDs; bleeding and perforation are its dangerous complications.

subject: Pathology I
question: Classify cirrhosis of the liver by morphology and aetiology. Describe its gross and microscopic features.

diagram.caption: Microscopic picture of cirrhosis
labels: separated by bridging fibrous septa containing inflammatory cells and proliferating bile ducts

answer_html:
Definition Cirrhosis is a diffuse, irreversible process of the liver characterised by fibrosis and conversion of normal liver architecture into structurally abnormal regenerative nodules. It is the end stage of many chronic liver diseases.

A. Classification 1. Morphological (2 marks) | Type | Nodule size | Common cause | |---|---|---| | Micronodular | Less than 3 mm, uniform | Alcoholic cirrhosis (early), haemochromatosis, biliary obstruction | | Macronodular | More than 3 mm, variable | Post-viral hepatitis (B, C), Wilson's disease, late alcoholic | | Mixed | Both | Many causes |

2. Aetiological

  1. Alcoholic liver disease – major cause.
  2. Chronic viral hepatitis – B, C (and D) – very important in India.
  3. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (obesity, diabetes, metabolic syndrome) – rapidly increasing.
  4. Biliary – primary biliary cholangitis, secondary to long-standing obstruction (stones, strictures, biliary atresia).
  5. Metabolic/genetic – haemochromatosis (iron), Wilson's disease (copper), α1-antitrypsin deficiency.
  6. Autoimmune hepatitis.
  7. Cardiac (long-standing right heart failure), drugs and toxins (methotrexate), Budd–Chiari syndrome.
  8. Cryptogenic (unknown cause).

B. Pathogenesis (brief) Repeated hepatocyte death → activation of hepatic stellate (Ito) cells into collagen-producing myofibroblasts → fibrous septa link portal tracts and central veins → surviving hepatocytes regenerate as nodules → disturbed blood flow → portal hypertension.

C. Gross features (3 marks)

  • Liver may be enlarged early (fatty, alcoholic), but usually becomes shrunken, firm and nodular.
