  • Surface is irregular and nodular ("hobnail liver" in alcoholic cirrhosis); cut surface shows nodules separated by grey-white fibrous bands.
  • Colour – yellow-tan (fatty), green (bile-stained), brown.

D. Microscopic features

  1. Regenerative nodules (pseudolobules) of hepatocytes without normal central veins.
  2. Bridging fibrous septa (delicate or broad) surrounding the nodules.
  3. Chronic inflammatory cells (lymphocytes) in septa; bile duct proliferation.
  4. Features of cause – fatty change and Mallory–Denk bodies (alcohol), ground-glass hepatocytes (HBV), iron or copper deposits.
  5. Loss of normal lobular architecture.

E. Complications

  • Portal hypertension – ascites, oesophageal varices (haematemesis), splenomegaly, caput medusae, haemorrhoids.
  • Liver failure – jaundice, bleeding tendency, hepatic encephalopathy, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hepatorenal syndrome, spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynaecomastia.
  • Hepatocellular carcinoma; infections (spontaneous bacterial peritonitis).

Nursing relevance Abstinence from alcohol, hepatitis B vaccination, salt restriction and diuretics for ascites, monitoring for GI bleeding and confusion, lactulose for encephalopathy.

Conclusion Cirrhosis is diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodules caused mainly by alcohol and viral hepatitis in India, leading to portal hypertension and liver failure.

subject: Pathology I
question: Write a note on the pathology of diabetes mellitus and its complications.
answer_html:
Introduction Diabetes mellitus (DM) is a group of metabolic disorders characterised by chronic hyperglycaemia due to defects in insulin secretion, insulin action, or both. India has one of the largest numbers of diabetics in the world. The biochemical features and types were studied earlier; pathology focuses on changes in the pancreas and the long-term damage to blood vessels and organs.

1. Pathology of the pancreas

  • Type 1 DM – autoimmune destruction of β-cells; islets show insulitis (lymphocytic infiltration) and marked reduction in β-cells.
  • Type 2 DM – insulin resistance with relative β-cell failure; islets show amyloid deposition and a modest reduction of β-cells.

2. Mechanisms of chronic complications

  • Advanced glycation end-products (AGEs) – glucose binds to proteins, damaging vessel walls and basement membranes.
  • Polyol (sorbitol) pathway – sorbitol accumulates in nerves, lens and retina (osmotic damage).
  • Activation of protein kinase C, oxidative stress, and inflammation.

3. Macrovascular disease

  • Accelerated atherosclerosis of large and medium arteries →
    • Coronary artery disease, myocardial infarction (commonest cause of death in diabetics).
    • Stroke.
    • Peripheral vascular disease → gangrene of the feet.

4. Microvascular disease (diabetic microangiopathy)

  • Thickening of capillary basement membranes and hyaline arteriolosclerosis. (a) Diabetic nephropathy

  • Diffuse glomerulosclerosis and nodular glomerulosclerosis (Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules) – pathognomonic.

  • Arteriolosclerosis, pyelonephritis, renal papillary necrosis.

  • Clinically – microalbuminuria → proteinuria → nephrotic syndrome → chronic kidney failure. (b) Diabetic retinopathy

  • Non-proliferative – microaneurysms, dot-and-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots, macular oedema.

  • Proliferative – new vessel formation, vitreous haemorrhage, retinal detachment → blindness.

  • Also cataract and glaucoma. (c) Diabetic neuropathy

  • Peripheral symmetrical sensory neuropathy ("glove and stocking" numbness, burning feet) → painless foot ulcers.

  • Autonomic neuropathy – postural hypotension, gastroparesis, bladder dysfunction, erectile dysfunction.

5. Infections Increased risk of tuberculosis, urinary tract infections, skin infections, candidiasis, mucormycosis and diabetic foot infections (impaired neutrophil function and poor circulation).

6. Acute complications (brief) Diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state, hypoglycaemia (due to treatment).

Nursing relevance Good glycaemic and BP control, annual eye and urine albumin checks, daily foot inspection and care, smoking cessation, early treatment of infections.

Conclusion Chronic hyperglycaemia damages large and small blood vessels through glycation and other pathways, causing heart disease, stroke, nephropathy, retinopathy, neuropathy and infections – most of which can be delayed by good control.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the pathogenesis and pathology of acute osteomyelitis.
answer_html:
Definition Osteomyelitis is inflammation of bone and bone marrow, almost always due to infection, most commonly by pyogenic bacteria.

1. Routes of infection

  1. Haematogenous – from a distant focus (boil, tonsillitis, umbilical sepsis) through blood – commonest in children.
  2. Direct – compound fractures, gunshot wounds, surgery (orthopaedic implants).
  3. Contiguous spread – from adjacent infection (diabetic foot ulcer, dental abscess, pressure sores).

2. Causative organisms

  • Staphylococcus aureus – most common (80–90%).
  • Streptococci, E. coli (neonates, elderly), Salmonella (sickle cell disease), Pseudomonas (puncture wounds), H. influenzae (young children).
  • M. tuberculosis – tuberculous osteomyelitis (spine – Pott's disease).

3. Pathogenesis of acute haematogenous osteomyelitis

  1. Bacteria settle in the metaphysis of long bones (lower femur, upper tibia), where blood flow is sluggish in looped capillaries.
  2. Acute inflammation → pus formation; pressure rises in the rigid bone, compressing vessels → ischaemic necrosis of bone.
  3. Pus spreads through Haversian canals to the surface → lifts the periosteum → subperiosteal abscess (periosteum stripped → more bone death).
  4. The dead piece of bone separates – sequestrum.
  5. The elevated periosteum forms new bone around the dead bone – involucrum.
  6. Openings in the involucrum through which pus escapes – cloacae; pus tracks to the skin – discharging sinus.
  7. In infants, infection may enter the joint (septic arthritis) and damage the growth plate.

4. Clinical features Sudden high fever, toxaemia, severe localised bone pain, tenderness, refusal to move the limb (pseudoparalysis in infants), swelling and warmth.

5. Investigations Raised WBC, ESR and CRP; blood culture (positive in about half); X-ray changes appear only after 10–14 days (periosteal reaction, lytic areas); MRI detects early changes; aspiration/biopsy for culture.

6. Chronic osteomyelitis and complications

  • Results from inadequately treated acute infection – persistent sequestra, sinuses, recurrent flare-ups.
  • Brodie's abscess – a localised chronic bone abscess.
  • Complications: septicaemia, pathological fracture, septic arthritis, growth disturbance, amyloidosis, squamous cell carcinoma in long-standing sinus tracts.

Nursing relevance Early IV antibiotics for 4–6 weeks, rest and splintage of the limb, pain relief, aseptic sinus dressing, nutrition, and care after surgical drainage/sequestrectomy.

Conclusion Acute osteomyelitis, mostly staphylococcal, begins in the metaphysis and produces pus, sequestrum and involucrum; early diagnosis and antibiotics prevent chronicity.

subject: Pathology I
question: Define goitre. Classify goitre and describe the pathology of simple (colloid) goitre.
answer_html:
Definition Goitre is an enlargement of the thyroid gland, of any cause. It may be associated with normal (euthyroid), increased (hyperthyroid) or decreased (hypothyroid) function.

1. Classification (a) Simple (non-toxic) goitre

  • Diffuse non-toxic (colloid) goitre.
  • Multinodular goitre (later stage).

  • Causes:

    • Endemic – iodine deficiency (sub-Himalayan belt, hilly regions of India).
    • Sporadic – physiological demand (puberty, pregnancy), goitrogens (cabbage, cauliflower, cassava, some drugs – lithium), inherited defects of hormone synthesis (dyshormonogenesis). (b) Toxic goitre (with hyperthyroidism)

  • Graves' disease (diffuse toxic goitre – autoimmune; TSH-receptor-stimulating antibodies).

  • Toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma. (c) Inflammatory goitre (thyroiditis)

  • Hashimoto's thyroiditis (autoimmune – lymphocytic infiltration; leads to hypothyroidism), de Quervain's (subacute) thyroiditis. (d) Neoplastic

  • Follicular adenoma; carcinoma – papillary (commonest), follicular, medullary, anaplastic.

2. Pathogenesis of simple goitre

  1. Iodine deficiency or other causes → reduced thyroid hormone synthesis.
  2. Low T3/T4 → increased TSH secretion from the pituitary.
  3. TSH causes hypertrophy and hyperplasia of thyroid follicles → diffuse enlargement (hyperplastic stage).
  4. When demand falls or iodine improves, follicles fill with colloid (colloid involution stage).
  5. Repeated cycles of hyperplasia and involution → uneven growth, nodules, haemorrhage, fibrosis, calcification and cyst formation → multinodular goitre.

3. Pathology

  • Diffuse colloid goitre – gross: symmetrically enlarged, soft, smooth gland; cut surface brown, glassy (colloid).
  • Microscopy: early – crowded small follicles lined by tall columnar cells (hyperplasia); later – large follicles distended with colloid, lined by flattened epithelium.
  • Multinodular goitre – gross: asymmetric, nodular gland (may weigh several hundred grams), with haemorrhage, scarring, calcification and cysts; microscopy – follicles of varying size, some with abundant colloid, areas of fibrosis and haemorrhage.

4. Effects Cosmetic swelling, pressure symptoms (dysphagia, breathlessness/stridor, hoarseness), retrosternal extension, occasionally hyperthyroidism (toxic nodule); simple goitre is usually euthyroid. In endemic areas, iodine deficiency in pregnancy causes cretinism and lower IQ in children.

5. Prevention and nursing relevance

  • Iodised salt under the National Iodine Deficiency Disorders Control Programme (at least 15 ppm iodine at consumer level); store salt in closed containers away from moisture and add it after cooking.
  • Pre- and post-thyroidectomy care when surgery is required.

Conclusion Goitre has many causes; simple goitre, mainly due to iodine deficiency, evolves from diffuse hyperplasia to colloid and multinodular goitre and is preventable with iodised salt.

subject: Pathology I
question: Write the stages of lobar pneumonia.
answer_html:
Stages of lobar pneumonia (classically in untreated pneumococcal pneumonia):

  1. Congestion (days 1–2) – engorged capillaries; alveoli contain oedema fluid, few neutrophils and many bacteria.
  2. Red hepatisation (days 2–4) – alveoli filled with neutrophils, red cells and fibrin; lobe red, firm, liver-like; rusty sputum.
  3. Grey hepatisation (days 4–8) – red cells disintegrate; fibrin and neutrophils remain; lobe greyish-brown and dry.
  4. Resolution (from day 8–9) – exudate digested by enzymes and cleared by macrophages; lung returns to normal. Early antibiotics shorten or prevent these stages.

subject: Pathology I
question: Enlist four causes of peptic ulcer.
answer_html:
Causes of peptic ulcer

  1. Helicobacter pylori infection (most important).
  2. NSAIDs and aspirin (reduce protective prostaglandins).
  3. Hyperacidity – Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma).
  4. Smoking and alcohol.
  5. Stress ulcers – severe burns (Curling's ulcer), head injury (Cushing's ulcer), critical illness.
  6. Corticosteroids (especially with NSAIDs), genetic factors (blood group O), chronic diseases (cirrhosis, COPD, kidney failure).

Pathogenesis in one line: ulcers form when aggressive factors (acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) overcome mucosal defences (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins, blood flow). Most ulcers heal when H. pylori is eradicated and NSAIDs are stopped.

subject: Pathology I
question: List any four complications of diabetes mellitus.
answer_html:
Complications of diabetes mellitus Acute

  1. Diabetic ketoacidosis; hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state.

  2. Hypoglycaemia (due to treatment). Chronic

  3. Diabetic nephropathy (Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodules → kidney failure).

  4. Diabetic retinopathy (blindness), cataract.
  5. Diabetic neuropathy – peripheral and autonomic.
  6. Macrovascular disease – coronary artery disease, stroke, peripheral vascular disease, diabetic foot and gangrene.
  7. Infections – tuberculosis, UTI, mucormycosis, skin infections.
  8. Cataract, periodontal disease, erectile dysfunction.

Prevention: good control of blood sugar (HbA1c below about 7%), BP and lipids; stopping smoking; annual eye, urine albumin and foot checks.

subject: Pathology I
question: Write the laboratory findings in acute pancreatitis.
answer_html:
Laboratory findings in acute pancreatitis

  1. Serum amylase – raised (usually more than 3 times normal) within 6–12 hours; returns to normal in 3–5 days.
  2. Serum lipase – raised; more specific and remains elevated longer (7–14 days).
  3. Leukocytosis; raised CRP (high values after 48 hours indicate severe disease).
  4. Hyperglycaemia (damage to islets, stress).
  5. Hypocalcaemia (calcium used in fat necrosis – saponification; a sign of severity).
  6. Raised bilirubin, ALP and ALT in gallstone pancreatitis; raised LDH, urea and creatinine in severe cases; low PaO₂.
  7. Imaging – ultrasound (gallstones), contrast CT (necrosis, complications).

subject: Pathology I
question: Define bronchiectasis.
answer_html:
Bronchiectasis is the permanent, abnormal dilatation of bronchi and bronchioles caused by destruction of the muscle and elastic tissue of their walls, resulting from chronic necrotising infection or obstruction.

Causes: post-infectious (tuberculosis, measles, whooping cough, severe pneumonia), bronchial obstruction (tumour, foreign body), cystic fibrosis, Kartagener syndrome (immotile cilia), immunodeficiency. Features: chronic cough with large amounts of foul-smelling purulent sputum (worse on changing posture, in the morning), haemoptysis, clubbing, recurrent infections; usually affects lower lobes. Complications: lung abscess, empyema, brain abscess, amyloidosis, cor pulmonale.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the steps in the estimation of haemoglobin by Sahli's method.

diagram.caption: Sahli's haemoglobinometer
labels: comparator box with brown glass standards

answer_html:
Introduction Haemoglobin (Hb) estimation is the commonest test for detecting anaemia. Sahli's (acid haematin) method is a simple, inexpensive visual method still used in many peripheral laboratories and wards, though automated analysers and digital haemoglobinometers are now preferred.

1. Principle Haemoglobin is converted to brown-coloured acid haematin by adding N/10 (0.1 N) hydrochloric acid. The acid haematin solution is then diluted with distilled water until its colour matches the standard brown glass of the comparator. The Hb value is read directly from the graduated tube.

2. Requirements

  • Sahli's haemoglobinometer – comparator with standard brown glass rods, graduated Sahli tube (in g/dl and %), Sahli pipette (marked at 20 µl = 0.02 ml), glass stirrer, dropper.
  • N/10 HCl, distilled water, sterile lancet, 70% spirit swabs, cotton, blotting paper, gloves.

3. Procedure

  1. Explain the procedure; wash hands and wear gloves.
  2. Fill the Sahli tube with N/10 HCl up to the lowest mark (2 g% mark/10% mark).
  3. Clean the fingertip (side of the ring finger) with spirit and allow to dry.
  4. Prick with a sterile lancet to get a free flow of blood; wipe away the first drop (contains tissue fluid).
  5. Draw blood exactly up to the 20 µl mark of the pipette without air bubbles; wipe the outside of the tip.
  6. Blow the blood into the acid at the bottom of the tube and rinse the pipette by sucking and expelling the acid 2–3 times; mix with the stirrer.
  7. Allow to stand for 10 minutes for complete formation of acid haematin.
  8. Add distilled water drop by drop, mixing after each addition, and compare the colour with the standard in natural daylight.
  9. Stop when the colour exactly matches the standard; read the lower meniscus of the fluid (in g/dl).
  10. Dispose of the lancet in a sharps container; record the result.

4. Normal values

  • Adult men: 13–17 g/dl; adult women: 12–15 g/dl; newborn: 14–20 g/dl; children: 11–13 g/dl.
  • WHO anaemia cut-offs: below 13 g/dl (men), below 12 g/dl (non-pregnant women), below 11 g/dl (pregnant women and children 6–59 months).

5. Sources of error and limitations

  • Subjective colour matching (eye fatigue, poor light, colour blindness).
  • Fading of the standard; acid haematin colour develops slowly (reading too early gives low values).
  • Not all forms of Hb (carboxy-Hb, met-Hb) are converted.
  • Inaccurate blood volume (air bubbles, clots), dilution of the sample by squeezing the finger.
  • Error of about ±10%.
  • Better methods: cyanmethaemoglobin method (reference), automated haematology analysers, digital haemoglobinometers (used in Anaemia Mukt Bharat).

Nursing relevance Nurses may perform Hb estimation in wards and community camps; correct technique, infection control and interpretation help detect anaemia early.

Conclusion Sahli's method converts Hb into acid haematin and estimates it by visual comparison – simple and cheap, but less accurate than modern methods.

subject: Pathology I
question: Write a note on cardiac biomarkers.
answer_html:
Definition Cardiac biomarkers are substances released into the blood when the heart muscle is injured or stressed. Their measurement helps in the diagnosis, risk assessment and monitoring of acute coronary syndromes, myocardial infarction (MI) and heart failure.

1. Markers of myocardial injury (necrosis) | Marker | Rises | Peaks | Returns to normal | Comments | |---|---|---|---|---| | Cardiac troponins (cTnI, cTnT) | 3–4 hours (high-sensitivity assays within 1–3 hours) | 24–48 hours | 7–14 days | Most sensitive and specific; marker of choice; useful for late diagnosis | | CK-MB | 4–6 hours | 12–24 hours | 2–3 days | Useful to detect re-infarction | | Myoglobin | 1–3 hours (earliest) | 6–12 hours | 24 hours | Not specific (also in skeletal muscle injury) | | LDH (LDH-1) | 12–24 hours | 2–3 days | 8–14 days | Old marker, rarely used now |

2. Markers of cardiac stress – natriuretic peptides

  • B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) and NT-proBNP are released from ventricles when they are stretched (volume or pressure overload).
  • Uses: diagnosis of heart failure in breathless patients (a normal value makes heart failure unlikely), assessing severity and prognosis, monitoring treatment.

3. Other markers

  • High-sensitivity CRP – inflammation; predicts cardiovascular risk.
  • D-dimer – helps exclude pulmonary embolism/DVT (not a cardiac marker but used in chest pain evaluation).

4. Interpretation

  • Diagnosis of acute MI requires a rise and/or fall of cardiac troponin with at least one value above the upper reference limit (99th percentile), plus symptoms of ischaemia, ECG changes or imaging evidence.
  • Serial samples are needed (e.g., at presentation and after 1–3 hours with high-sensitivity assays, or 3–6 hours with conventional assays).
  • Troponin may also rise in myocarditis, pulmonary embolism, sepsis, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, cardiac surgery and after defibrillation.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Note the time of onset of chest pain and the time of each sample.
  • Collect blood in the correct tube (plain/serum or heparin as per laboratory), label with date and time, send immediately; follow up results urgently.
  • Repeat samples at the ordered intervals; continue ECG monitoring.

Conclusion Troponins are the gold-standard markers of myocardial injury, CK-MB helps detect re-infarction, and BNP/NT-proBNP reflect heart failure – together they guide rapid diagnosis and treatment.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the complete blood count – its components, normal values and clinical significance.
answer_html:
Introduction The complete blood count (CBC) is the most frequently ordered laboratory test. Done on an automated haematology analyser using EDTA blood, it gives information about red cells, white cells and platelets, helping to diagnose anaemia, infection, inflammation, leukaemia and bleeding disorders.

1. Sample

  • 2–3 ml venous blood in an EDTA (lavender/purple) tube; mix gently by inverting 8–10 times (prevents clotting); send within 2–4 hours.

2. Components and normal values (adults) | Parameter | Normal value | |---|---| | Haemoglobin | Men 13–17 g/dl; women 12–15 g/dl | | RBC count | Men 4.5–5.5 million/µl; women 3.8–4.8 million/µl | | Haematocrit (PCV) | Men 40–50%; women 36–46% | | MCV (mean corpuscular volume) | 83–101 fl | | MCH (mean corpuscular haemoglobin) | 27–32 pg | | MCHC | 31.5–34.5 g/dl | | RDW (red cell distribution width) | 11.6–14% | | Total leucocyte count (TLC) | 4,000–11,000/µl | | Differential count | Neutrophils 40–80%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 2–10%, eosinophils 1–6%, basophils 0–2% | | Platelet count | 1.5–4.5 lakh/µl (150,000–450,000/µl) |

3. Clinical significance (a) Red cells

  • Low Hb – anaemia. RBC indices classify it:
    • Microcytic hypochromic (low MCV, MCH) – iron deficiency, thalassaemia, anaemia of chronic disease.
    • Macrocytic (high MCV) – vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease, alcoholism.
    • Normocytic – acute blood loss, haemolysis, chronic disease, kidney failure.

  • High Hb/PCV – dehydration, dengue (haemoconcentration), polycythaemia, smokers, high altitude. (b) White cells

  • Leucocytosis – neutrophilia in bacterial infections, MI, burns, steroids; lymphocytosis in viral infections, TB, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia; eosinophilia in allergy, asthma, worm infestations (common in India); monocytosis in TB, recovery phase of infections.

  • Leucopenia – viral infections (dengue), typhoid, drugs (chemotherapy, antithyroid drugs), aplastic anaemia, HIV.

  • Very high counts with abnormal cells – leukaemia. (c) Platelets

  • Thrombocytopenia – dengue, malaria, ITP, DIC, drugs (heparin), leukaemia, aplastic anaemia – risk of bleeding.

  • Thrombocytosis – iron deficiency, infection, after splenectomy, myeloproliferative disorders.

4. Nursing responsibilities Correct tube and volume, avoid prolonged tourniquet and haemolysis, label properly, note drugs and transfusions, recognise critical values (e.g., Hb below 7 g/dl, platelets below 20,000/µl, TLC below 1,000/µl) and report immediately; neutropenic and bleeding precautions as needed.

Conclusion The CBC is a simple yet powerful test; correct collection and interpretation guide diagnosis and nursing care in many diseases.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) – methods, factors affecting it and clinical significance.
answer_html:
Definition The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is the rate at which red blood cells settle down in a column of anticoagulated blood kept vertically in a standard tube, measured in millimetres at the end of the first hour (mm/1st hour). It is a simple, non-specific indicator of inflammation and tissue damage.

1. Mechanism (stages)

  1. Rouleaux formation – RBCs stack like coins (promoted by fibrinogen and globulins).
  2. Sedimentation – rouleaux settle rapidly.
  3. Packing – cells pack at the bottom slowly.

2. Methods (a) Westergren method (recommended)

  • 2 ml venous blood + 0.5 ml of 3.8% sodium citrate (4:1 ratio).
  • Fill the Westergren tube (200 mm long) up to the zero mark; keep it exactly vertical in a stand at room temperature, away from vibration and sunlight.
  • Read the height of the clear plasma column after 1 hour.

  • Normal: men 0–15 mm/hour, women 0–20 mm/hour (increases with age). (b) Wintrobe method

  • EDTA/oxalated blood in a 100 mm Wintrobe tube; reading after 1 hour; the same tube can be centrifuged for PCV.

  • Normal: men 0–9 mm, women 0–20 mm. (Automated ESR analysers are also used.)

3. Factors affecting ESR Increased ESR

  • Increased fibrinogen and globulins – infections, inflammation.
  • Anaemia (fewer cells settle faster), macrocytosis.
  • Pregnancy, old age, female sex.

  • Tilted tube, high room temperature. Decreased ESR

  • Polycythaemia, abnormal RBC shapes (sickle cells, spherocytes) that prevent rouleaux.

  • Low fibrinogen, very high WBC counts.
  • Delay in testing, low temperature, clotted sample.

4. Clinical significance

  • Raised in: tuberculosis (used to monitor response), acute and chronic infections, rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, rheumatic fever, multiple myeloma (often above 100 mm/hour), cancers, myocardial infarction, temporal arteritis and polymyalgia rheumatica (very high).
  • Uses: to detect hidden inflammatory disease, to monitor disease activity and treatment response (TB, RA).
  • Limitations: non-specific – a normal ESR does not rule out disease; C-reactive protein rises and falls faster.

5. Nursing responsibilities Collect into the correct citrate tube in the right ratio, mix gently, avoid clotting and haemolysis, send promptly (within 2 hours), and record the patient's age, sex and pregnancy status.

Conclusion ESR is a cheap, simple marker of inflammation; its value lies in monitoring disease activity rather than in making a specific diagnosis.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the preparation and uses of a peripheral blood smear.

diagram.caption: Preparation of a thin peripheral blood smear
labels: drop of blood near one end
body and tail; area for examination near tail

answer_html:
Introduction A peripheral blood smear (blood film) is a thin layer of blood spread on a glass slide, stained and examined under the microscope. It shows the shape, size and colour of blood cells and detects parasites – information that automated counters cannot fully give.

1. Sample

  • Capillary blood (finger prick) or EDTA venous blood (smear made within 2–3 hours).

2. Preparation of a thin smear

  1. Use clean, grease-free slides; label one end.
  2. Place a small drop of blood about 1–2 cm from one end of the slide.
  3. Hold a spreader slide at an angle of 30–45° in front of the drop, draw it back to touch the drop and let the blood spread along its edge.
  4. Push the spreader forward in one smooth, quick movement – a tongue-shaped smear with a head, body and tail is formed (about two-thirds of the slide).
  5. Air-dry quickly (wave the slide); do not heat.
  6. Fix with methanol (Leishman stain contains methanol) and stain with Leishman's stain (or Giemsa/Field's/JSB stain) as per method; wash with buffered water and dry.
  7. Examine under oil immersion, in the thin area near the tail where cells just touch each other. - Thick smear (for malaria) – a larger drop spread in a small circle, dried and stained without fixing; RBCs lyse, concentrating parasites.

3. Uses (a) Red cell morphology

  • Size and colour – microcytic hypochromic (iron deficiency), macrocytes (B12/folate deficiency).
  • Shape – sickle cells (sickle cell anaemia), target cells (thalassaemia, liver disease), spherocytes (hereditary spherocytosis), schistocytes/fragmented RBCs (DIC, haemolytic uraemic syndrome), nucleated RBCs.

  • Inclusions – basophilic stippling (lead poisoning), Howell–Jolly bodies (after splenectomy). (b) White cells

  • Differential leucocyte count; detection of blast cells (leukaemia), atypical lymphocytes (viral infections, dengue), toxic granules (sepsis), hypersegmented neutrophils (B12/folate deficiency). (c) Platelets

  • Estimation of number, clumps and giant platelets. (d) Parasites

  • Malaria parasites (species identification on thin smear), microfilariae (night blood smear collected between 10 pm and 2 am), Babesia, trypanosomes.

4. Nursing responsibilities Correct collection (finger prick with free flow, first drop wiped), timely smear for malaria (before antimalarials, preferably during fever), night samples for filaria, proper labelling and prompt delivery to the laboratory.

Conclusion The peripheral smear is a cheap, informative test that reveals anaemia types, leukaemias, platelet problems and blood parasites.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the tests for bleeding and coagulation disorders and the nurse's role.
answer_html:
Introduction Haemostasis depends on blood vessels, platelets and clotting factors. Tests of bleeding and coagulation help to diagnose bleeding disorders (haemophilia, ITP, DIC, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency), to monitor anticoagulant therapy, and to check safety before surgery and invasive procedures.

1. Tests of vessel and platelet function

  • Platelet count – normal 1.5–4.5 lakh/µl; bleeding risk increases below 50,000 and spontaneous bleeding below about 10,000–20,000/µl.
  • Bleeding time (BT) – time taken for a small skin puncture to stop bleeding; Duke's method (ear lobe/finger) normal 1–5 minutes; Ivy method (forearm with BP cuff at 40 mmHg) 2–7 minutes. Prolonged in thrombocytopenia, platelet function defects, von Willebrand disease, aspirin use.
  • Tourniquet (Hess) test – capillary fragility; used in dengue (petechiae counted in a marked square below the cuff).
  • Clot retraction, platelet function tests.

2. Tests of coagulation

  • Clotting time (CT) – time for blood to clot in a glass tube; normal 5–10 minutes (Lee–White); crude test, prolonged in severe factor deficiencies.
  • Prothrombin time (PT) – tests the extrinsic and common pathways (factors VII, X, V, II, fibrinogen); normal about 11–16 seconds.
    • Reported as INR (International Normalised Ratio) – normal about 1.0; target 2–3 for warfarin therapy.
    • Prolonged in warfarin therapy, liver disease, vitamin K deficiency (including newborn), DIC.
  • Activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) – tests the intrinsic and common pathways (XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, II); normal about 25–40 seconds.
    • Prolonged in haemophilia A and B, heparin therapy (kept at 1.5–2.5 times control), DIC, liver disease.
  • Thrombin time, fibrinogen level (200–400 mg/dl).
  • D-dimer and FDPs – raised in DVT, pulmonary embolism and DIC.
  • Specific factor assays (factor VIII, IX) – diagnosis of haemophilia.

3. Interpretation (brief) | Condition | Platelets | BT | PT | aPTT | |---|---|---|---|---| | Thrombocytopenia/ITP | Low | Prolonged | Normal | Normal | | Haemophilia | Normal | Normal | Normal | Prolonged | | Warfarin/vitamin K deficiency | Normal | Normal | Prolonged | Normal/prolonged | | Liver disease, DIC | Normal/low | Normal/prolonged | Prolonged | Prolonged |

4. Nurse's role

  1. Sample collection – sodium citrate 3.2% (light-blue top) tube, filled exactly to the mark (9:1 ratio); mix gently; avoid prolonged tourniquet; do not draw from a heparinised line; send within 1–4 hours.
  2. Note the time of the last heparin/warfarin dose on the form.
  3. Bleeding precautions in patients with abnormal results – avoid IM injections, apply pressure on puncture sites for 5–10 minutes, soft toothbrush, watch for gum bleeding, haematuria, black stools, petechiae.
  4. Ensure tests are done before surgery, liver biopsy, lumbar puncture, epidural catheter insertion/removal.
  5. Report critical values (e.g., INR above 5, platelets below 20,000/µl).

Conclusion Platelet count, BT, PT/INR and aPTT together identify the cause of bleeding and guide anticoagulant therapy; correct sample collection by the nurse ensures reliable results.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain blood grouping and cross-matching.
answer_html:
Introduction Safe blood transfusion depends on giving blood that is compatible with the recipient. Blood grouping identifies the ABO and Rh groups, and cross-matching (compatibility testing) confirms that donor red cells will not react with antibodies in the recipient's serum. (The physiology of the ABO system was studied earlier; here we focus on laboratory methods.)

A. ABO blood grouping 1. Forward (cell) grouping

  • Patient's red cells are tested with known anti-A and anti-B (and anti-AB) sera.

  • Agglutination with anti-A → group A; with anti-B → group B; with both → AB; with neither → O. 2. Reverse (serum) grouping

  • Patient's serum/plasma is tested with known A cells and B cells.

  • Detects naturally occurring anti-A/anti-B antibodies; results must agree with forward grouping (double check against errors). 3. Methods

  • Slide method – rapid, for screening/emergencies.

  • Tube method – more reliable, standard in blood banks; gel/column agglutination in modern laboratories.

B. Rh (D) typing

  • Red cells tested with anti-D serum; agglutination = Rh-positive.
  • Rh-negative donors are tested for weak D.
  • Important in transfusion and in pregnancy (Rh-negative mother – anti-D prophylaxis).

C. Antibody screening

  • The patient's serum is screened against panel red cells for unexpected antibodies (from previous transfusions or pregnancies).

D. Cross-matching (compatibility testing) 1. Major cross-match (most important)

  • Recipient's serum + donor's red cells. 2. Minor cross-match (rarely done now)

  • Donor's plasma + recipient's red cells. 3. Phases

  • Immediate spin (saline, room temperature) – detects ABO incompatibility (IgM antibodies).

  • 37 °C incubation with enhancing media (albumin, LISS).

  • Antiglobulin (indirect Coombs) phase – detects incomplete IgG antibodies (e.g., Rh, Kell). 4. Result

  • No agglutination or haemolysis = compatible; the unit is labelled for that patient.

  • In extreme emergencies, O-negative packed red cells may be issued before cross-matching (with the doctor's written request).

E. Sources of error Clerical errors (wrong labelling, wrong patient) are the commonest cause of ABO-incompatible transfusion – more than technical errors.

F. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Identify the patient with two identifiers; label the sample at the bedside immediately after collection; one patient at a time.
  2. Use the correct tube (EDTA/plain as per blood bank) and complete the requisition form fully.
  3. A fresh sample is required if the patient has been transfused or was pregnant in the last 3 months (sample usually valid for 72 hours).
  4. Two-person bedside check of patient and blood unit before transfusion; close monitoring during transfusion.

Conclusion Forward and reverse grouping, Rh typing and cross-matching ensure that the right blood reaches the right patient; careful labelling by the nurse is the most important safety step.

subject: Pathology I
question: Describe the blood components, their storage and indications.
answer_html:
Introduction Modern blood banks separate donated whole blood into components – packed red cells, platelets, plasma and cryoprecipitate. Component therapy gives each patient only what he needs, so one donation can help several patients, with fewer reactions and less volume overload.

1. Whole blood

  • About 350–450 ml with anticoagulant (CPDA-1); stored at 2–6 °C for 35 days.
  • Rarely used now – acute massive blood loss when components are not available.

2. Packed red blood cells (PRBC)

  • Red cells after removing most plasma (haematocrit 55–75%); additive solution (SAGM) extends storage to 42 days at 2–6 °C.
  • Indications: symptomatic anaemia, acute blood loss, surgery, thalassaemia; one unit raises Hb by about 1 g/dl in adults.
  • Special forms – leucodepleted (fewer febrile reactions), irradiated (prevents transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease in immunocompromised), washed cells.

3. Platelet concentrates

  • Random donor platelets (RDP) from whole blood, or single donor platelets (SDP) by apheresis (equal to 5–6 RDP units).
  • Storage: 20–24 °C with continuous gentle agitation, for 5 days – never refrigerate.
  • Indications: thrombocytopenia with bleeding (dengue with bleeding, leukaemia, chemotherapy, DIC), prophylaxis when count is very low (e.g., below 10,000/µl), before surgery with low platelets.
  • One RDP raises the count by about 5,000–10,000/µl.

4. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)

  • Plasma separated and frozen within 6–8 hours of collection; stored at −18 °C or colder (preferably −30 °C) for up to 1 year; thawed at 30–37 °C and used promptly.
  • Contains all clotting factors.
  • Indications: bleeding with multiple clotting factor deficiencies – liver disease, DIC, massive transfusion, warfarin reversal (if prothrombin complex concentrate is unavailable), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (plasma exchange).
  • Not for volume expansion or nutrition.

5. Cryoprecipitate

  • Cold-insoluble portion of FFP rich in factor VIII, fibrinogen, von Willebrand factor and factor XIII; stored frozen.
  • Indications: low fibrinogen (DIC, massive bleeding, obstetric haemorrhage), von Willebrand disease and haemophilia A when factor concentrates are unavailable.

6. Plasma derivatives

  • Albumin, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), factor VIII and IX concentrates, anti-D immunoglobulin.

7. Compatibility rules (brief)

  • Red cells – ABO and Rh compatible (O negative = universal red-cell donor).
  • Plasma – ABO compatible with recipient's red cells (AB plasma = universal plasma donor).

8. Nursing responsibilities Collect components just before use; start within 30 minutes of issue and complete red cells within 4 hours; platelets and FFP over a shorter time as ordered; use a standard blood set with filter; never refrigerate platelets or refreeze plasma; monitor for reactions; document unit numbers.

Conclusion Each component has its own storage and indications; component therapy uses scarce blood efficiently and safely.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the types of transfusion reactions and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction A transfusion reaction is any adverse event associated with transfusion of blood or its components. Most are mild, but some – especially ABO-incompatible haemolytic reactions – can be fatal. Early recognition and correct management by the nurse are life-saving. Reactions are reported to the Haemovigilance Programme of India.

A. Acute reactions (within 24 hours) 1. Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction

  • Cause: ABO-incompatible blood, usually due to clerical/identification error; recipient antibodies destroy donor red cells inside vessels.

  • Features: start within minutes – fever, chills, pain at the infusion site, back/loin pain, chest tightness, flushing, breathlessness, hypotension, haemoglobinuria (dark urine), oliguria (acute kidney injury), DIC (oozing from puncture sites). 2. Febrile non-haemolytic reaction (commonest)

  • Due to cytokines/antibodies against donor white cells; rise in temperature of ≥1 °C with chills; prevented by leucodepleted blood. 3. Allergic (urticarial) reaction

  • Reaction to donor plasma proteins – itching, hives, rash; usually mild. 4. Anaphylactic reaction

  • Severe – bronchospasm, hypotension, shock (e.g., IgA-deficient patients). 5. Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI)

  • Within 6 hours – acute breathlessness, hypoxia, fever, hypotension due to donor antibodies damaging lung capillaries (non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema). 6. Transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO)

  • Too much or too fast transfusion in elderly, infants, heart/kidney patients – breathlessness, cough, crepitations, raised BP and JVP. 7. Bacterial contamination (septic reaction)

  • High fever, rigors, shock – especially with platelets (stored at room temperature). 8. Metabolic – hypothermia (cold blood given fast), hyperkalaemia, hypocalcaemia (citrate toxicity) in massive transfusion; air embolism.

B. Delayed reactions

  • Delayed haemolytic reaction (3–14 days) – fever, jaundice, falling Hb (antibodies from previous transfusion/pregnancy).
  • Transfusion-transmitted infections – HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, malaria (all donated blood is screened for these in India).
  • Transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (prevented by irradiated blood), post-transfusion purpura, iron overload in repeatedly transfused patients (thalassaemia – chelation therapy), alloimmunisation.

C. Management (general steps for any suspected acute reaction)

  1. Stop the transfusion immediately; do not discard the bag.
  2. Keep the IV line open with normal saline (using a new set).
  3. Check patient identity and the unit label again at the bedside.
  4. Monitor vital signs, oxygen saturation, urine output; inform the doctor and blood bank at once.
  5. Send the blood bag with the set, fresh blood samples (EDTA and plain) and the first urine sample to the blood bank for investigation (repeat grouping, cross-match, direct Coombs test, haemoglobinuria).
  6. Treat as ordered:
    • Fever – antipyretics; allergic – antihistamines; anaphylaxis – adrenaline IM, oxygen, fluids.
    • Haemolytic – fluids to maintain urine output, diuretics, treat DIC and kidney injury.
    • TACO – sit upright, oxygen, diuretics; TRALI – oxygen/ventilatory support.
  7. Document and complete the transfusion reaction report (haemovigilance).

Prevention Correct identification at sample collection and bedside, slow start with close observation in the first 15 minutes, correct rate, use of leucodepleted/irradiated components when indicated.

Conclusion Transfusion reactions range from mild fever and itching to fatal haemolysis; most serious reactions are preventable by correct identification and close monitoring.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the routine examination of urine and its clinical significance.
answer_html:
Introduction Urine routine examination is a simple, cheap and very informative test that gives clues to diseases of the kidneys, urinary tract, liver and metabolism (diabetes). It includes physical, chemical and microscopic examination.

1. Sample collection

  • Fresh, early-morning, clean-catch mid-stream urine (10–20 ml) in a clean, dry, wide-mouthed container; examined within 1–2 hours (or refrigerated) – otherwise cells and casts break down and bacteria multiply.

2. Physical examination | Feature | Normal | Abnormal and significance | |---|---|---| | Volume (24 h) | 800–2,500 ml | Polyuria (>3 l) – diabetes mellitus/insipidus; oliguria (<400 ml) – dehydration, acute kidney injury; anuria (<100 ml) | | Colour | Pale yellow (urochrome) | Dark yellow – concentrated, bilirubin (jaundice); red – haematuria, haemoglobinuria, beetroot; orange – rifampicin; brown/black – myoglobin, alkaptonuria; milky – chyluria (filariasis), pus | | Appearance | Clear | Turbid – pus, phosphates, bacteria | | Odour | Aromatic | Ammoniacal (stale urine, UTI); fruity (ketones) | | Specific gravity | 1.003–1.030 | High – dehydration, glycosuria; low – diabetes insipidus; fixed at 1.010 – chronic kidney disease | | pH | 4.5–8 (about 6) | Alkaline in UTI (urea-splitting organisms), acidic in acidosis |

3. Chemical examination (often by dipstick)

  • Protein (heat and acetic acid test, sulphosalicylic acid test, dipstick) – proteinuria in glomerulonephritis, nephrotic syndrome, diabetic nephropathy, pre-eclampsia, UTI.
  • Sugar (glucose) – Benedict's test (green → yellow → orange → brick-red with increasing sugar) or glucose oxidase dipstick – glycosuria in diabetes mellitus, renal glycosuria, pregnancy.
  • Ketone bodies – Rothera's test (purple ring) – diabetic ketoacidosis, starvation, persistent vomiting.
  • Bile salts (Hay's test) and bile pigments (Fouchet's test) – obstructive jaundice; urobilinogen – raised in haemolytic jaundice, absent in obstructive jaundice.
  • Blood – haematuria, haemoglobinuria, myoglobinuria.
  • Nitrite and leucocyte esterase – suggest urinary tract infection.

4. Microscopic examination (centrifuged deposit)

  • Pus cells – normal 0–5/high-power field; increased in UTI.
  • Red cells – normal 0–2/HPF; increased in stones, glomerulonephritis, tumours, TB, trauma.
  • Epithelial cells.
  • Casts – hyaline (normal, concentrated urine), RBC casts (glomerulonephritis), WBC casts (pyelonephritis), granular (acute tubular necrosis), waxy (chronic kidney failure), fatty (nephrotic syndrome).
  • Crystals – calcium oxalate (envelope-shaped), uric acid, triple phosphate (coffin-lid), cystine – kidney stones.
  • Bacteria, yeasts, Trichomonas, ova of Schistosoma.

5. Nursing responsibilities Teach the correct mid-stream technique, label the sample, send promptly; for 24-hour urine – discard the first morning sample, collect all urine for the next 24 hours including the next morning's first sample, in a container with preservative, kept cool; record the total volume.

Conclusion Physical, chemical and microscopic examination of urine detects kidney disease, diabetes, jaundice and infection – a simple test with great diagnostic value.

subject: Pathology I
question: Explain the normal composition of CSF and the CSF findings in different types of meningitis.
answer_html:
Introduction Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is obtained by lumbar puncture. Its examination is essential for diagnosing meningitis, encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage and some neurological diseases. Rapid and correct handling of the sample can save lives.

1. Normal CSF (adult) | Parameter | Normal | |---|---| | Appearance | Clear, colourless ("gin-clear") | | Opening pressure (lying) | About 50–180 mm of water | | Cells | 0–5 lymphocytes/µl; no neutrophils or RBCs | | Protein | 15–45 mg/dl | | Glucose | 50–80 mg/dl (about 60–70% of blood glucose) | | Chloride | 120–130 mEq/l | | Gram stain/culture | Negative |

2. CSF findings in meningitis | Feature | Acute bacterial (pyogenic) | Tuberculous | Viral | |---|---|---|---| | Appearance | Turbid/purulent | Clear or slightly turbid; cobweb clot (pellicle) on standing | Clear | | Pressure | Markedly raised | Raised | Normal or slightly raised | | Cells | 1,000–5,000+/µl, mainly neutrophils | 50–500/µl, mainly lymphocytes | 10–500/µl, lymphocytes | | Protein | Markedly raised (100–500 mg/dl) | Markedly raised | Normal or mildly raised | | Glucose | Very low (<40 mg/dl; CSF/blood ratio <0.4) | Low | Normal | | Special tests | Gram stain, culture, latex antigen tests | ZN stain (low yield), CBNAAT, culture, raised ADA | PCR for viruses |

3. Other findings

  • Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV) – lymphocytes, low glucose, India ink preparation and cryptococcal antigen positive.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage – uniformly blood-stained CSF in all tubes, xanthochromia (yellow supernatant) after a few hours; a traumatic tap clears in successive tubes.
  • Guillain–Barré syndrome – raised protein with normal cell count (albuminocytological dissociation).

4. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Explain the procedure, obtain consent, ask the patient to empty the bladder.
  2. Position – lateral with knees drawn to the chest and chin flexed (or sitting bent forward); support the patient throughout.
  3. Maintain strict asepsis; collect CSF in sterile, numbered tubes; send a simultaneous blood glucose sample.
  4. Transport immediately at room temperature – never refrigerate (meningococci and Haemophilus die in the cold).
  5. After the procedure – observe for headache, CSF leak, bleeding, neurological changes and vital signs; encourage fluids.

5. Collection order of tubes (commonly) Tube 1 – biochemistry (protein, glucose); Tube 2 – microbiology (Gram stain, culture, CBNAAT); Tube 3 – cell count; Tube 4 – special tests (cytology, PCR) – as per laboratory policy.

Conclusion Cell type, protein and glucose in CSF distinguish bacterial, tuberculous and viral meningitis; prompt, correct handling of the sample is vital.

subject: Pathology I
question: Differentiate between transudate and exudate.
answer_html:
Introduction Abnormal collections of fluid in body cavities – pleural effusion, ascites, pericardial effusion – or in tissues may be transudates or exudates. Distinguishing them by fluid analysis tells the doctor whether the cause is systemic (pressure imbalance) or local (inflammation, infection, cancer).

1. Definitions

  • Transudate – a protein-poor, cell-poor fluid formed because of imbalance of hydrostatic and oncotic pressures with normal vessel permeability.
  • Exudate – a protein-rich, cell-rich fluid formed because of increased vascular permeability due to inflammation or invasion.

2. Differences | Feature | Transudate | Exudate | |---|---|---| | Mechanism | ↑ hydrostatic pressure or ↓ oncotic pressure | ↑ vascular permeability (inflammation) | | Appearance | Clear, pale yellow | Cloudy, turbid, purulent or blood-stained | | Specific gravity | Below 1.012 | Above 1.020 | | Protein | Below 3 g/dl | Above 3 g/dl | | Fluid/serum protein ratio | Below 0.5 | Above 0.5 | | LDH | Low (fluid/serum LDH below 0.6) | High (above 0.6) | | Cells | Few (mesothelial cells) | Many – neutrophils (bacterial), lymphocytes (TB, cancer) | | Glucose | Same as plasma | May be low (TB, empyema, rheumatoid arthritis) | | Clotting on standing | Does not clot | Clots (fibrinogen present) | | Causes | Heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition (hypoalbuminaemia) | Tuberculosis, pneumonia, cancer, pancreatitis, rheumatoid arthritis, pulmonary embolism |

3. Light's criteria (pleural fluid is an exudate if any one is present)

  1. Pleural fluid protein / serum protein > 0.5.
  2. Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH > 0.6.
  3. Pleural fluid LDH more than two-thirds of the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

4. Additional tests on body fluids

  • Adenosine deaminase (ADA) – raised in tuberculous effusion.
  • Cytology – malignant cells.
  • Gram stain, ZN stain, culture, CBNAAT.
  • Amylase (pancreatitis), triglycerides (chylous effusion).
  • For ascites – serum–ascites albumin gradient (SAAG): ≥1.1 g/dl suggests portal hypertension (cirrhosis).

5. Nursing responsibilities Prepare and position the patient for thoracentesis/paracentesis, maintain asepsis, collect fluid into the required containers (plain, EDTA, culture bottles), send a simultaneous blood sample for protein/LDH/glucose, label and dispatch quickly, and monitor the patient afterwards (breathing, BP, site).

Conclusion Transudates point to systemic causes such as heart failure or cirrhosis, while exudates indicate local disease such as TB, infection or cancer – Light's criteria help to tell them apart.

subject: Pathology I
question: What is a reticulocyte count? State its significance.
answer_html:
Reticulocytes are young (immature) red blood cells that still contain remnants of RNA, seen as a blue network (reticulum) with supravital stains (new methylene blue or brilliant cresyl blue).

Normal count: 0.5–2.5% of red cells in adults (2–6% in newborns).

Significance – index of bone marrow erythropoietic activity:

  • Increased (reticulocytosis): haemolytic anaemia, after acute blood loss, and response to treatment of iron, B12 or folate deficiency (peaks in 5–10 days) – used to check that therapy is working.
  • Decreased: aplastic anaemia, marrow infiltration (leukaemia), untreated nutritional anaemias, chronic kidney disease.

question: List the anticoagulants used in blood collection tubes with their colour codes and uses.
answer_html:
Tube colour Additive Main uses
Lavender/purple EDTA CBC, peripheral smear, HbA1c, blood grouping (blood bank)
Light blue Sodium citrate 3.2% (9:1) PT/INR, aPTT, coagulation tests
Black Sodium citrate 3.8% (4:1) ESR (Westergren)
Grey Sodium fluoride + potassium oxalate Blood glucose (fluoride stops glycolysis), lactate
Green Heparin Plasma chemistry, electrolytes; heparinised syringe for ABG
Red/yellow (gel) No anticoagulant/clot activator Serum – LFT, RFT, serology, hormones

Order of draw: blood culture bottles → citrate → serum (plain) → heparin → EDTA → fluoride – prevents carry-over of additives.

subject: Pathology I
question: Who are the universal donor and the universal recipient?
answer_html:
For red cell transfusion

  • Universal donor – group O Rh-negative: red cells have no A, B or D antigens, so they are not destroyed by the recipient's anti-A or anti-B antibodies. Used in extreme emergencies before grouping.
  • Universal recipient – group AB Rh-positive: plasma has no anti-A or anti-B antibodies, so the person can receive red cells of any ABO group.

For plasma transfusion the rule reverses – AB plasma can be given to all groups (universal plasma donor) and group O persons can receive plasma of any group.

Note: whenever possible, group-specific, cross-matched blood is always given.

subject: Pathology I
question: What is haematocrit (packed cell volume)? Give its normal values and significance.
answer_html:
Haematocrit (packed cell volume, PCV) is the percentage of the total blood volume occupied by red blood cells, measured after centrifuging anticoagulated blood (Wintrobe or micro-haematocrit tube) or calculated by automated analysers.

Normal values: men 40–50%; women 36–46%; newborn 50–60%.

Significance

  • Raised: dehydration (burns, diarrhoea), dengue fever – a rise of 20% or more indicates plasma leakage (warning sign), polycythaemia, high altitude.
  • Reduced: anaemia, haemodilution (excess IV fluids, pregnancy), after haemorrhage (once fluid shifts).
  • Used to monitor fluid therapy in dengue and burns.
